target.title: fix: prevent doctor hangs on large Memory Core migrations
target.body:
Closes #108442

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running `openclaw doctor --fix` during an upgrade with a large legacy Memory Core index could see hours of full-core CPU use, multi-gigabyte WAL growth, and no completed migration.

## Why This Change Was Made

The sidecar migration performed one full FTS5 scan per legacy chunk because the FTS `id` column is intentionally `UNINDEXED`. This change materializes overlapping FTS identities and exact-match status with one ordered FTS scan, then uses ordinary primary-key lookups to preserve canonical conflicts and copy only absent rows.

The existing single-savepoint, canonical-wins, rollback, and source-archive contracts remain unchanged. This PR does not add batching, resumability, or progress reporting.

## User Impact

Large legacy Memory Core indexes can migrate without the quadratic FTS validation phase that made `doctor --fix` appear hung. Existing atomic rollback and conflict behavior remain the same.

## Evidence

- Synthetic 10,000-row comparison on Apple Silicon, Node 24.18.0, SQLite 3.53.2:
  - Previous validator: 6,355 ms
  - Indexed materialization: 13 ms
  - Observed speedup: 508x
- `/opt/homebrew/opt/node@24/bin/node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.test.ts`
  - 37 tests passed
- `/opt/homebrew/opt/node@24/bin/node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-core/src/migration/legacy-memory-sidecar-fts.test.ts`
  - Query-plan regression passed
- Targeted `oxfmt`, `oxlint`, `git diff --check`, and production extension typecheck passed.
- The extension-test typecheck is blocked by the pre-existing `extensions/kimi-coding/kimi-coding.live.test.ts` import of missing `isLiveTestEnabled`; the same failure reproduces on clean `main` at `5a0fcc2ff92`.
- Structured Codex autoreview: no findings, patch correct at 0.94 confidence.

AI-assisted with Codex. The implementation, tests, dependency contracts, and review findings were verified before commit.

I’m using the OpenClaw debugging workflow to separate observed behavior from the owning code path, Martian Learn for the repository’s authorized project context, and the technical-writing style guide for the final report. I’ll diagnose only; I won’t change code or external state.

Martian Memory policy denies project-specific reads for this repository, so I’m continuing without them. The debugging skill’s required references are local repository docs; I’m reading those before tracing the gist’s exact failure path.

The gist contains three artifacts: a user-facing report and two raw troubleshooting transcripts. I’m treating the report as a hypothesis and the transcripts as evidence, then I’ll trace the implicated SQLite startup paths in this checkout.

The new trace changes the diagnosis materially: `plugins list --verbose` reaches the final plugin table and returns to PowerShell. The discovery scans take tens of milliseconds, so the original “all plugin commands hang” claim is not supported by that captured run. I’m splitting the code trace into command bootstrap, SQLite migration/locking, and downgrade/plugin-state paths.

The code path matches an existing cluster of startup-migration reports, including a strict gate that treats migration warnings as fatal. I’m invoking the OpenClaw maintainer issue workflow now because checking those live issues and their resolution status is part of distinguishing the actual defect from the plugin symptoms. This remains read-only.

The evidence now points to a startup-preflight failure, not a plugin-discovery hang. I’m checking the matching issue history and post-beta fixes now so the report distinguishes the proven failure path from plausible lock owners.

One more separation is emerging: the reported “doctor exit hang” may have been silent Memory Core migration work after the cron box, since that box is emitted before the rest of the migration graph finishes. I’m checking the Codex temp-tree ownership separately so it does not get blamed for an unrelated database path.

I’ve reconciled the apparent contradictions. There are two likely migration outcomes: a bounded lock failure while the custom cleanup task owns the agent database, and, once unlocked, a silent all-at-once import that can look hung for a long time. I’m doing the final evidence and repository-state checks now.

## Conclusion

This is not primarily a plugin-discovery hang. The gist describes four separate problems, with one main causal chain:

1. The manual `.clawdbot` merge exposed a legacy Memory Core SQLite sidecar.
2. Several commands automatically run legacy-state migration before doing their advertised work.
3. That migration first collided with another process holding `openclaw-agent.sqlite`.
4. Once unlocked, the migration could enter a large, silent, all-at-once SQLite import that looks hung.
5. Gateway startup treats any unresolved migration warning as fatal, so it never reaches plugin convergence.
6. Rolling back afterward created a separate, deterministic schema-version incompatibility.

### What the code proves

`plugins list`, `plugins update`, and bare `gateway` all enter config/state preflight in `2026.7.2-beta.1`. `gateway status --deep` is explicitly routed around that guard.

That perfectly explains why status worked while the operational commands appeared stuck. See:

- `src/cli/command-catalog.ts:162`
- `src/cli/command-catalog.ts:169`
- `src/cli/command-catalog.ts:380`
- `src/cli/program/config-guard.ts:161`
- `src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts:359`

The “Config warnings” panel prints before state migration starts. Full doctor also prints the cron migration result before awaiting the remaining state migrations. Therefore, the report’s “hung after Config warnings” and “hung on exit after Doctor changes” descriptions do not establish an exit/terminal-rendering bug. The process may still have been inside Memory Core migration.

### The two likely Memory Core outcomes

First, the exact warning:

> `Skipped Memory Core legacy memory index import ... because the sidecar could not be imported: Error: database is locked`

comes from the outer catch in `extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.ts:1242` at `a911e58`. An error during the actual sidecar ATTACH/copy transaction would say `because legacy rows could not be imported`.

That localizes the observed lock to canonical database setup, most likely acquiring/migrating `openclaw-agent.sqlite` or registering it in shared state. Ryan independently observed that the custom `OpenClaw Session Store Cleanup Guard` respawned a process and re-locked that exact database. That scheduled script is the strongest lock-holder candidate.

The lock itself is bounded by a five-second SQLite busy timeout. The attached verbose trace confirms that run did not hang: it printed the lock warning, printed all 75 plugins, and returned to the PowerShell prompt.

Second, once the external lock clears, the importer can take a much worse path. At `a911e58`, `importLegacyMemorySidecarIndex` copies and validates the entire legacy database inside one SAVEPOINT:

- no batching
- no intermediate commits
- no progress reporting
- no resume cursor
- no WAL checkpointing

That is `extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.ts:522-579`. This matches open issue [#108442](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/108442), where a 5.6 GB sidecar ran for nearly two hours while producing a 3.9 GB WAL and no externally visible committed rows.

Ryan only reports a roughly 4 GB state directory, not the sidecar’s exact size, CPU usage, or live WAL growth. So I cannot prove he hit the same long transaction. It is, however, the strongest source-backed explanation for commands becoming silent immediately after the preflight panel.

### Why Gateway stayed down

Bare Gateway startup requires a successful startup-migration checkpoint. At `src/commands/doctor-config-preflight.ts:434-452`, any migration warning prevents readiness. It also skips plugin convergence while such warnings exist.

Consequently:

- A locked agent database blocks Gateway readiness.
- An unlocked but large sidecar can keep Gateway silent inside migration.
- Brave, Codex, and Discord remain old because startup never reaches convergence.
- `gateway status --deep` succeeding says nothing about migration health because that command bypasses the guard.

### What is not the cause

- **Plugin discovery:** The lifecycle trace shows scans and registry construction completing in roughly 20–93 ms. The full listing returns to the prompt.
- **DeepSeek warning:** This is stale config for a missing plugin. It is noisy but not blocking.
- **Codex’s doubled `plugins/plugins` path:** This is expected. Codex checks out `openai/plugins` at `.tmp/plugins`, and that repository contains `plugins/<name>`, yielding `.tmp/plugins/plugins/nvidia/...`. The installed Codex version defines this at [Codex `startup_sync.rs:23-27`](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.134.0/codex-rs/core-plugins/src/startup_sync.rs#L23-L27), with the inner layout demonstrated in [its tests](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.134.0/codex-rs/core-plugins/src/startup_sync_tests.rs#L22-L59). The long path can break older Windows copy tools, but it is not runaway recursion.
- **Missing WAL/SHM files:** That does not disprove a lock. SQLite uses OS file locks, and journal sidecars depend on journal mode and connection state. [SQLite locking documentation](https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html).
- **A leaked SQLite handle:** Possible elsewhere, but weakly supported. The relevant target handle, ATTACH, transaction, timers, and migration lease all have cleanup paths.

### Plugin drift is real but secondary

Brave, Codex, and Discord remained on `[REDACTED_PHONE]-beta.1` while core moved to `2026.7.2-beta.1`. A global `npm install` updates core without necessarily converging external plugins.

Those old packages passed the beta’s compatibility gates and were successfully listed. They can still cause plugin-specific runtime bugs, especially Codex version skew, but they do not explain the preflight behavior or schema errors.

Post-beta [PR #107691](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/107691) fixes a related stale-managed-plugin condition, but Ryan’s trace contains none of its characteristic `ENOTDIR` failures.

### The rollback problem is

[assistant]
I’m treating this as two separate questions: whether #108442 covers Ryan’s long silent import, and whether a testable PR can also address his earlier lock/readiness failure. I’m using the OpenClaw issue-maintainer and debugging workflows, plus the repository’s memory-policy check, to verify current issue state and the exact fix boundary before I answer.

Martian Memory policy is disabled for this repository, so I’m continuing without project-specific memory. The issue workflow also requires a cached issue search first; that tool was missing earlier, so I’ll verify that and then use live GitHub data if it remains unavailable.

Issue #108442 is open and unassigned, with a source-level reproduction but a maintainer decision flagged around atomic versus resumable migration. Per the maintainer workflow, I’m assigning it to you (`@jalehman`) before going deeper; no labels, comments, or code will be changed.

The key distinction is already clear: #108442 can plausibly explain Ryan’s long, silent migration phase, but it cannot explain away the separate writer holding `openclaw-agent.sqlite`. I’m checking whether the right fix is really “batch the import” or whether this legacy database is entirely rebuildable index state—which would lead to a much safer fix.

I found a sharper source-level defect than the issue currently describes: the FTS copy/verification looks up each chunk by `id`, but that FTS5 column is deliberately `UNINDEXED`. SQLite therefore scans the whole FTS table for every chunk—roughly quadratic work. At 184k chunks, that is on the order of tens of billions of comparisons. I’m validating that query plan now; batching alone would leave the main pathology intact.

The query-plan test confirms it. On a tiny synthetic fixture, doubling rows from 2,500 → 5,000 → 10,000 made the current validation take 0.35s → 1.39s → 5.51s (quadratic), while an indexed snapshot path handled 100,000 rows in 0.14s. That gives us a narrow trial-PR shape that keeps the existing atomic transaction and conflict semantics.

Short answer: a fix for #108442 may be necessary for Ryan, but it would not be sufficient. He appears to have two sequential blockers:

1. A competing process locks `openclaw-agent.sqlite`.
2. Once that lock clears, a large legacy index may hit #108442’s pathological import.

## A concrete cause for #108442

I found a more specific defect than “the transaction is too large.”

`copyLegacyMemoryFtsRows()` performs two correlated lookups against `memory_index_chunks_fts.id` for every legacy chunk: [extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.ts:391](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/14bb0b4e526d77eacfe26340fee7635c902f0a3e/extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.ts#L391).

But `id` is declared `UNINDEXED`: [packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/memory-schema.ts:676](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/14bb0b4e526d77eacfe26340fee7635c902f0a3e/packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/memory-schema.ts#L676). SQLite explicitly says `UNINDEXED` values are not added to the FTS index. [SQLite FTS5 documentation](https://www.sqlite.org/fts5.html#the_unindexed_column_option)

`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` confirms that each lookup performs:

```text
CORRELATED SCALAR SUBQUERY
SCAN canonical VIRTUAL TABLE INDEX 0
```

A `SCAN` means visiting the complete table rather than using a selective lookup. [SQLite query-plan documentation](https://sqlite.org/eqp.html#table_and_index_scans)

My synthetic benchmark demonstrates quadratic scaling:

| Rows | Current validation | Indexed snapshot |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2,500 | 352 ms | — |
| 5,000 | 1,386 ms | — |
| 10,000 | 5,506 ms | 13 ms |
| 100,000 | impractical | 142 ms |

The #108442 reporter had about 184,000 chunks. The two correlated FTS passes can therefore perform on the order of 34 billion candidate comparisons. That fits the reported hours of high CPU extremely well. The encompassing savepoint separately explains the multi-gigabyte WAL and zero externally visible rows: [extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.ts:530](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/14bb0b4e526d77eacfe26340fee7635c902f0a3e/extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.ts#L530).

This changes my fix recommendation. I would not start by implementing resumable batching. A narrower first PR can retain atomicity:

- Snapshot existing FTS `(id, rowid)` pairs into a temporary ordinary table.
- Add a B-tree index on the temporary `id`.
- Use it for conflict and missing-row checks.
- Fetch existing FTS rows by `rowid` when comparing exact values.
- Preserve the existing canonical-FTS-wins behavior and outer savepoint.
- Add overlap/conflict tests plus a multi-thousand-row/query-plan regression.

That likely removes the dominant pathological behavior without forcing the larger atomic-versus-resumable product decision. If WAL size remains unacceptable afterward, resumable staging becomes a separate follow-up.

## Does that solve Ryan?

Not completely.

Ryan’s captured warning is:

```text
because the sidecar could not be imported: Error: database is locked
```

That wording comes from the outer migration catch at `extensions/memory-core/doctor-contract-api.ts:1241`, not the inner row-copy catch. It therefore does not establish that the bulk import was even reached.

Moreover, the complete `plugins list --verbose` trace in [Ryan’s gist](https://gist.github.com/jalehman/8754a3d2b42974d3382197ed522fda72) prints the entire plugin table and returns to PowerShell. That particular run did not hang.

The strongest separate suspect is `OpenClaw Session Store Cleanup Guard`. It is not part of this repository, and Ryan reports that it respawned a Node process and re-locked `openclaw-agent.sqlite`.

| Observation | Meaning | Fixed by #108442 PR? |
|---|---|---|
| High CPU plus growing destination WAL | Quadratic FTS import | Likely |
| Outer `database is locked` warning | Competing writer/setup contention | No |
| Full plugin list plus PowerShell prompt | Command completed | Nothing to fix there |
| Stable reading beta-upgraded schemas | Unsupported downgrade | No |

## What to request from Ryan

I would send him this:

> Please don’t rerun this against your only live state. Could you send:
>
> 1. The exact size of `.openclaw\memory\main.sqlite`, plus any `-wal`, `-shm`, `.migrated`, or retry copies. The report only gives the total `.openclaw` size.
> 2. Read-only row counts for `files`, `chunks`, `embedding_cache`, and `chunks_vec` if present.
> 3. During an actually silent run, two snapshots 15 seconds apart showing the OpenClaw Node PID, accumulated CPU time, and sizes of `openclaw-agent.sqlite`, `-wal`, and `-shm`.
> 4. The process holding `openclaw-agent.sqlite`, using Resource Monitor or:
>
> ```powershell
> handle64.exe -nobanner "openclaw-agent.sqlite"
> ```
>
> 5. The sanitized contents of `clawd\scripts\ops\openclaw-session-store-cleanup.ps1`, plus the scheduled task’s trigger and action.
> 6. The exact final output line and whether the Node process still exists while the terminal appears stuck.
>
> Please don’t upload the SQLite files; they contain indexed private content.

The decisive split is simple:

- CPU and WAL steadily rising: he has reached #108442.
- Stable WAL plus another PID holding the file: lock-owner problem.
- No Node process while PowerShell remains blocked: wrapper/terminal-return problem.

## PR readiness

Yes—I now have enough for a focused trial PR, tentatively `fix(memory): avoid quadratic FTS sidecar migration`.

I would base it on current `main`, which already contains merged [#108652](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/108652) and [#108663](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/108663). I would be comfortable handing that build to Ryan only with these conditions:

- Run against a copied state directory.
- Stop the Gateway and cleanup scheduled task first.
- Preserve the July 12 backup.
- Expect current `main` to advance SQLite schemas, making another stable downgrade unsafe.
- Record elapsed time, CPU, WAL growth, and final row counts.

target.title: fix: keep /think and /verbose session prefs past freshness gate
target.body:
Closes #109275

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who set `/think` or `/verbose` on a session could see those stored preferences dropped during agent-command session resolution whenever lifecycle freshness failed (for example when a terminal main transcript is newer than the registry snapshot, or after implicit session rotation). The preferences remained in the session store, but `persistedThinking` / `persistedVerbose` were gated on `fresh` and became `undefined`, so later turns fell through to agent/provider defaults instead of the session override.

## Why This Change Was Made

Session freshness should only control session-id reuse and rollover. Stored thinking and verbose levels are user session preferences and must still be exposed to the agent-command resolution chain whenever the session entry still carries them. The fix keeps the existing `fresh` lifecycle path, and only removes that gate from preference reads. Explicit per-turn overrides remain higher priority via `thinkOnce ?? thinkOverride ?? persistedThinking`.

Compatibility: no config/API shape change; only restores intended preference propagation for existing session store fields. Performance: no extra I/O or hot-path discovery. Usability: `/think` / `/verbose` continue to mean “for this session” across turns. Security: no trust-boundary change; preferences already trusted from the local session store.

## User Impact

After `/think high` (or `/verbose …`) is stored on a session, later agent-command turns continue to honor that level even when session lifecycle marks the entry not-fresh. Operators no longer need to re-issue the directive after rotation/transcript freshness mismatches.

## Evidence

Verification host: local macOS (Crabbox bypass)

```text
# Focused primary + sibling
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  src/agents/command/session.provider-owned-reset.test.ts \
  src/agents/command/session.resolve-session-key.test.ts
# Test Files  2 passed (2)
# Tests       9 passed (9)

# Path-scoped format (oxfmt) on both touched files: clean
# git diff --check: clean
# pnpm check:changed: Plugin SDK API baseline failed (unrelated; this PR only touches
#   src/agents/command/session.ts + session.provider-owned-reset.test.ts)
# pnpm test:changed: stopped after heavy expansion into vitest.unit-fast; substituted focused path above
```

New regression cases in `session.provider-owned-reset.test.ts`:
1. Fresh active session still exposes stored `thinkingLevel` / `verboseLevel`
2. When terminal-transcript-newer forces `!fresh` + `isNewSession`, stored prefs still surface as `persistedThinking` / `persistedVerbose`

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: Session-stored `/think` and `/verbose` preferences remain available to agent-command resolution even when lifecycle freshness is false.
- Environment: local macOS OpenClaw checkout at branch `fix/109275-persisted-thinking-fresh-gate` (head `93fe5c7d2`), Node 24, focused Vitest via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs`.
- Current-main contrast: on `origin/main`, `resolveSession` computes `persistedThinking` / `persistedVerbose` only when `fresh && sessionEntry?.thinkingLevel|verboseLevel`. With stored `thinkingLevel: "high"` and `terminalTranscriptNewer=true` (forces `!fresh`), main returns `persistedThinking === undefined` while rotating the session id.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  ```bash
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/command/session.provider-owned-reset.test.ts
  ```
  Cases: “exposes stored thinking and verbose preferences when the session is still fresh” and “keeps stored thinking and verbose preferences when lifecycle marks the session not fresh”.
- Evidence after fix: both cases pass; not-fresh case asserts `isNewSession === true`, new `sessionId`, and still `persistedThinking === "high"` / `persistedVerbose === "full"`.
- Control check: provider-owned daily-boundary and model-locked session cases still pass unchanged; only preference reads are decoupled from `fresh`.
- Observed result after fix: stored session preferences propagate to `persistedThinking` / `persistedVerbose` regardless of lifecycle freshness; rollover still creates a new session id when appropriate.
- What was not tested: live multi-turn CLI chat against a real model provider; channel auto-reply paths that already read `sessionEntry.thinkingLevel` directly; full `pnpm test:changed` suite (substituted with focused session tests after heavy expansion).

target.title: feat: add LLMRouter provider plugin
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw has no provider plugin for [LLMRouter](https://llmrouter.sh), an OpenAI-compatible routing API. Compared to routing through a single fixed model or provider, it offers:

- Automatic routing to the lowest-cost model that still satisfies a given request's requirements (reasoning, code, tools, vision, context length)
- One OpenAI-compatible API surface for hundreds of models across providers, so a single integration covers them all
- Configurable SLAs that trade latency for lower pricing on non-urgent workloads
- A flat 1% platform fee on top of underlying model cost, versus OpenRouter's ~5%

Its headline feature is `model:"auto"` — routing every request to the cheapest model that meets the query's needs (similar in spirit to OpenRouter's `openrouter/auto`).

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds `extensions/llmrouter/` as an official external provider plugin, following the same shape as the most recently added comparable provider (Baseten, #108708):

- Provider id `llmrouter`, auth via `LLMROUTER_API_KEY` (`llmr_sk_...` bearer key), base URL `https://api.llmrouter.sh/v1`, `openai-completions` transport family.
- Default model `llmrouter/auto` — a single static catalog entry mirroring OpenRouter's own `openrouter/auto` (cost 0, conservative context/output defaults, since actual routing target/cost vary per request).
- Any other model id (e.g. `llmrouter/claude-opus-4-6`) resolves as a pinned pass-through slug via a dynamic resolver — LLMRouter exposes 500+ live registry slugs via `GET /v1/models`, so a static per-slug catalog isn't practical or accurate; this mirrors the same pattern Baseten and OpenRouter use for arbitrary/foreign model ids.
- Reasoning content is dropped across replayed turns, since `auto` can route different turns to different backend models and a prior turn's `reasoning_content` isn't safe to replay into an unrelated backend.

Wired into the repo the same way Baseten was: `.github/labeler.yml`, `package.json` dist-excludes, `scripts/lib/official-external-provider-catalog.json`, `docs/docs.json` nav, `docs/providers/index.md`, generated `docs/plugins/reference/llmrouter.md` + `plugin-inventory.md` + `docs_map.md` (via `pnpm plugins:inventory:gen` / `pnpm docs:map:gen`), and the zh-CN i18n glossary (`pnpm docs:check-i18n-glossary` passes clean).

## User Impact

Users can install `@openclaw/llmrouter-provider` and set `llmrouter/auto` as their default model to get LLMRouter's cost-aware auto-routing, or pin any specific upstream slug directly.

## Evidence

- Live-verified the API contract against a locally run instance of LLMRouter's `app.py`: confirmed `GET /v1/models` catalog shape (`auto` + slug list), `llmr_sk_...` bearer auth, and OpenAI-compatible error shapes (`401 invalid_api_key`, `402 insufficient_quota`) — matches the `openai-completions` transport family with no custom error handling needed.
- `extensions/llmrouter/index.test.ts` — 7 cases covering auth wizard metadata, static catalog shape, default-model onboarding, dynamic slug passthrough (including that it correctly yields to the static `auto` entry), replay policy, and modern-model-ref flag. All passing.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json` and `-p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json` — clean.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.extensions.json extensions/llmrouter` — clean.
- Ran `package-manifest.contract.test.ts`, `extension-runtime-dependencies.contract.test.ts`, `official-external-plugin-catalog.test.ts`, `official-external-provider-endpoints.test.ts`, `manifest-registry.test.ts`, `providers.test.ts` — all passing.
- `git diff --check` clean; all touched JSON files (`docs.json`, `official-external-provider-catalog.json`, glossary, package.json, plugin manifests) parse.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a GitHub Copilot embeddings request could echo credential-shaped text into user-visible error diagnostics. Both non-2xx paths in the Copilot embeddings integration (model discovery and the embeddings call itself) send a Copilot bearer token to a configurable base URL, then interpolate the bounded upstream response body verbatim into the thrown `Error`. If an upstream or proxy response reflected token-shaped or credential-shaped data, that content would surface unredacted in error messages, logs, and any operator-facing diagnostics for the Copilot embeddings provider.

## Why This Change Was Made

The two error paths now wrap the bounded response body read with `redactSensitiveText(...)` from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/logging-core` before interpolation. This is the established in-boundary SDK redaction helper already used by `extensions/crabbox`, so no new dependency or boundary crossing is introduced. The existing 8 KiB streaming read bound (`COPILOT_ERROR_BODY_LIMIT_BYTES`) is preserved, and the exact error message prefixes are unchanged (`GitHub Copilot model discovery HTTP <status>:` and `GitHub Copilot embeddings HTTP <status>:`). Preserving those prefixes is important because `isCopilotSetupError` matches on them for auto-selection fallback. Only the interpolated body segment is redacted; status codes and safe reason text are retained. Two short intent comments were added at the redaction sites.

## User Impact

Operators and developers using the GitHub Copilot embeddings provider get error diagnostics that no longer risk leaking credential-shaped upstream/proxy content, while keeping the same HTTP status and human-readable failure reason. There is no change to success paths, no change to error message prefixes, and no behavior change for Copilot setup detection or auto-selection fallback.

target.title: fix(line): dripping inbound media downloads hang past setup timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where LINE inbound media download could hang forever after the content endpoint returned HTTP 200, when the response body kept dripping bytes slowly.

Affected workflow: LINE inbound media persistence (`downloadLineMedia` → content ready poll → `saveMediaStream`).

## Why This Change Was Made

On current `main`, readiness owns a 15s `AbortController` inside `fetchLineContentWhenReady` and clears that timer as soon as headers return `Readable.fromWeb(response.body)`. After headers, only the Node stream remains — with no wall-clock — so a slow drip can keep `saveMediaStream` alive indefinitely.

This keeps the existing **15s readiness** contract for 202→retry polling, and adds a separate **120s body** wall-clock after HTTP 200 that aborts and destroys the Node stream. Body budget matches Slack/Feishu inbound media totals (`SLACK_MEDIA_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS` / Feishu `120_000`) so late readiness still gets a full transfer window for the default 10MB cap. LINE documents `api-data.line.me` as the large-data content endpoint where video/audio may spend time preparing before binary retrieval ([Get content](https://developers.line.biz/en/reference/messaging-api/#get-content)).

Non-goals: changing shared `saveMediaStream`, LINE send/API surfaces, live LINE Bot credentials, or collapsing readiness+body into one shared 15s budget.

**Collision check:** `path:extensions/line/src/download.ts` open PRs = 0 (all authors and Pick-cat).

## User Impact

- Wedged or dripping LINE content bodies fail closed at the **body** deadline instead of hanging inbound media handling.
- Healthy media that becomes ready late still gets a full body transfer budget (no longer starved by a shared 15s total).
- Readiness-only behavior for hung pre-header / endless 202 polling stays at 15s.

## Evidence

Exact head: `7f923be17856f009af73fc12858463fa97bcfd3f`.

### Timeout contract (post-fix)

| Phase | Budget | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Readiness | `CONTENT_READY_TIMEOUT_MS` = 15s | 202 polling until HTTP 200 headers |
| Body | `LINE_MEDIA_BODY_TIMEOUT_MS` = 120s | `saveMediaStream` after headers; stream destroyed on abort |

Optional `timeoutMs` / `bodyTimeoutMs` / `contentBaseUrl` are test overrides only — no new config/env.

### Observed real-behavior proof (local Vitest + `node:http` loopback)

Command:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/line/src/download.test.ts extensions/line/src/download.deadline.loopback.test.ts
```

Result at this head:

```text
✓ aborts a dripping content body within the body wall-clock deadline 474ms
✓ persists a slow-but-valid body before the body deadline 89ms
✓ aborts a hung content request at the readiness deadline 5ms
✓ aborts a dripping content body after headers within the body deadline 54ms
✓ keeps a fresh body deadline after late readiness 1ms
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  14 passed (14)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 4.83s
```

Concrete contract observations (not just green checks):

- **Body drip fail-closed:** real `node:http` peer returns HTTP 200 then drips 1 byte every 40ms; with `bodyTimeoutMs: 250`, rejection is `LINE media body for message mid-drip timed out after 0.25 seconds`, and wall-clock elapsed lands in `[200, 2000)` (observed ~474ms — bounded, not an indefinite hang).

target.title: fix(plugins): plugins.deny is bypassed by a mixed-case manifest id
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators who denylist a plugin would still have that plugin load in full, when the plugin's manifest declares its id in a different case than the denylist entry.

Plugin config policy lists are lowercase-normalized: `plugins.deny`, `plugins.allow`, and `plugins.entries` keys all pass through `normalizePluginId`, which trims and lowercases. A plugin's self-declared manifest id is only trimmed. So when an operator denylists `malicious-scraper` and a plugin publishes `"id": "Malicious-Scraper"`, the denylist comparison misses, no diagnostic is emitted, and the plugin falls through to default activation with its hooks, channels, secret provider integrations, and tools loaded. The operator sees the plugin listed as enabled with no indication their denylist entry did nothing.

The same gap applies to the core reserved-id check: a manifest declaring `"id": "Node-MCP"` evades the `CORE_RESERVED_PLUGIN_IDS` rejection that `node-mcp` would hit.

The allowlist side of the mismatch fails closed rather than open: a legitimately allowlisted plugin that declares a mixed-case id is blocked as `not-in-allowlist`.

## Why This Change Was Made

`src/plugins/manifest.ts:1787` mints `PluginManifestRecord.id`, the value every downstream policy consumer compares against config:

```ts
// before
const id = normalizeOptionalString(raw.id) ?? "";
```

`normalizeOptionalString` trims only, while `src/plugins/config-state.ts` normalizes every config-side id with `normalizeOptionalLowercaseString`. The two sides of each comparison are in different cases. The consumers that mismatch:

- `src/plugins/manifest-owner-policy.ts:57` - `normalizedConfig.deny.includes(params.plugin.id)`
- `src/plugins/config-activation-shared.ts:161` - `params.config.deny.includes(params.id)`

The fix canonicalizes at the parse boundary:

```ts
// after
const id = normalizeOptionalLowercaseString(raw.id) ?? "";
```

`manifest.ts` is the single point where a manifest id becomes a `PluginManifestRecord.id`, and `manifest-registry.ts` builds every record's `id` from that value. Canonicalizing here fixes the denylist check, the allowlist check, the per-entry `enabled: false` check, and the reserved-id check at once, rather than patching each comparison site and leaving the next one to re-introduce the gap. `normalizeOptionalLowercaseString` is the same trim-plus-lowercase helper the config side already uses.

Alias mapping deliberately stays out of the manifest path. `normalizePluginId` also resolves legacy config aliases, which is an input-normalization concern for operator-typed config, not for a manifest declaring its own identity.

Sibling manifest-id readers checked and unaffected:

- `src/plugins/manifest-metadata-scan.ts:197` uses a trimmed id purely as a local dedupe/ranking key within the scan, comparing raw ids to raw ids. It never reaches allow/deny policy.
- `src/plugins/installed-plugin-index-record-reader.ts:88` builds install-index records describing which packages are installed. Activation policy keys off `loadPluginManifest`, not this record.

Related but distinct: closed PR #59595 patched the same raw-vs-normalized class of mismatch at the `warnAboutUntrackedLoadedPlugins()` call site in `loader.ts`, for aliases, affecting a provenance warning. This change fixes the security-relevant deny/activation path at its source.

## User Impact

Operators who denylist a plugin now have that denylist honored regardless of the case the plugin author chose for its manifest id. A plugin can no longer self-select out of `plugins.deny` by publishing a mixed-case id, and cannot claim a mixed-case spelling of a core reserved id.

All 59 manifest ids shipped in this repo are already lowercase, so canonicalization is a no-op for every bundled plugin. Config-side behavior is untouched. Operators who had worked around the bug by adding a mixed-case denylist entry are unaffected, since config-side entries were already lowercased before comparison.

## Evidence

### Redacted live Gateway runtime inspection

A new integration fixture starts the real Gateway plugin bootstrap path through `loadPluginLookUpTable()` and `loadGatewayStartupPlugins()` with two on-disk bundled plugins:

- Denied manifest ID: `Denied-Fixture`; canonical runtime export ID: `denied-fixture`
- Allowed manifest ID: `Allowed-Fixture`; canonical runtime export ID: `allowed-fixture`
- Config: `allow: ["allowed-fixture"]`, `deny: ["denied-fixture"]`

Both fixtures attempt to register a legacy hook, typed Gateway hook, tool, channel, service, and secret-provider integration. The allowed fixture deliberately exports the canonical lowercase ID, exercising the loader's exact manifest/runtime ID contract.

The Gateway registry inspection asserts this redacted snapshot:

```json
{
  "deniedRegistryRecord": null,
  "imported": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "hooks": ["allowed-fixture", "allowed-fixture"],
  "tools": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "channels": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "services": ["allowed-fixture"],
  "secretIntegrations": ["allowed-fixture"]
}
```

This proves the denied mixed-case plugin is rejected before runtime registration: it has no registry record and contributes no imported runtime, hook, tool, channel, service, or secret-integration surface. The allowed mixed-case manifest loads successfully under the canonical `allowed-fixture` identity across every inspected surface.

Implementation: `src/gateway/server-plugin-bootstrap.browser-plugin.integration.test.ts`.

### Cold CLI-path regression context

The earlier on-disk CLI-path reproduction remains useful as the before/after activation check:

```text
# BEFORE (pristine main a8fe7dd834)
plugin id="Malicious-Scraper" enabled=true status="loaded"
# AFTER (patched tree, identical inputs)
plugin id="malicious-scraper" enabled=false status="disabled"
```

### Validation and branch status

- Rebased onto current `main` at `a327e43023cb9aa2e77162fc40a604655aa83557`.
- Current head: `3ca2ea71a40efad290cb1617bd6b6127326c184c`.
- Autoreview: clean; no actionable findings.
- The refreshed CI already cleared the original branch failures in `check-test-types` and `checks-node-compact-small-3` on the first refreshed head.
- `checks-node-compact-small-11` passed with the corrected live Gateway inspection: 128 Gateway-shard tests passed, including the denied/allowed surface proof.

Unit coverage also verifies lowercase identity, deny blocking, allow activation, disabled entries, reserved IDs, and unchanged lowercase IDs. The original manifest suite passed 132 focused assertions on Node 24 before the Gateway proof was added.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where music generation providers (for example fal) could hang forever when a CDN returned response headers and then dripped the audio body slowly enough to keep resetting the per-chunk idle timer. `fetchWithTimeout` clears its abort after headers land, so the download budget no longer applied to the body — including non-2xx error-detail reads inside shared `assertOkOrThrowHttpError`.

## Why This Change Was Made

At the `downloadGeneratedMusicAsset` call site only, keep one wall-clock deadline across headers + non-2xx error-detail + successful-body reads via `readResponseTextPrefix` / `readResponseWithLimit({ timeoutMs, onTimeout })`, matching the Vydra / Discord probe hang-floor shape.

Header fetch still goes through `fetchProviderOperationResponse` (keeps transient download retries). `requestFailedMessage` is omitted on purpose so shared `assertOkOrThrowHttpError` cannot consume a dripping error body without a wall-clock bound before this helper's timed readers run.

Collision check: no open hang-class PR on `downloadGeneratedMusicAsset` / `src/music-generation/provider-assets.ts`. Soft file overlap only with #107552 (base64 validation; different concern). #108982 is video-generation, not this helper.

## User Impact

target.title: fix(update): dev channel update builds from an unverified checkout at the git install path
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Package-to-dev conversion previously adopted whatever Git checkout already existed at `OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR`. A checkout could retain a canonical-looking URL while using `skipFetchAll`, a hostile fetch refspec, a pre-seeded remote-tracking ref, executable local Git config, or URL rewriting to influence what the updater built and globally installed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Remote validation cannot make an adopted checkout safe. This revision removes adoption entirely: package-to-dev conversion requires an unused path, creates a fresh checkout itself, and runs the clone plus all follow-up update/fetch commands with system, global, and injected Git configuration disabled. Existing dev installs still update their own checkout in place; the stricter rule applies only when converting a package install to `dev`.

If a conversion fails after doctor or the global-link step may have made the new path authoritative, OpenClaw records that checkout as conversion-owned. A retry stops the owned service, clones into a separate replacement directory, swaps only after the clone succeeds, and retires the replacement token after a successful conversion. Unrelated existing directories remain categorically rejected.

## User Impact

- `openclaw update --channel dev` from a package install now requires an unused `OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR`.
- Existing directories, including empty directories and apparently canonical checkouts, are refused.
- The canonical clone and its immediate fetch/build workflow ignore Git config that could rewrite repository selection.
- A failed updater-owned conversion can be retried without adopting its prior Git state or deleting the last service target before a replacement exists.
- Existing Git/dev installations are unchanged.

## Regression Coverage

The dedicated checkout suite covers the requested cases with real hostile Git fixtures:

- canonical URL plus `remote.origin.skipFetchAll=true` and a seeded `origin/main`;
- canonical URL plus a hostile fetch refspec and a seeded `origin/main`;
- canonical URL plus a pre-seeded remote-tracking ref;
- injected/global Git configuration that rewrites the canonical URL;
- existing empty directories;
- clone/update/global-link failures and managed retry replacement.

The command-level suite also verifies refusal occurs before service mutation, follow-up fetches receive the sanitized Git environment, failed initial conversions clean up safely, service-repair-aware failures retain a usable target, and successful conversion retires retry ownership.

## Evidence

Same package-to-dev entrypoint and same pre-seeded canonical-looking checkout; private paths and environment details are replaced with placeholders.

```text
BEFORE (origin/main)
$ OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR=<private>/checkout openclaw update --channel dev --yes
... existing checkout accepted ...
$ git -C <private>/checkout config remote.origin.skipFetchAll
true
$ git -C <private>/checkout rev-parse refs/remotes/origin/main
<pre-seeded-commit>
... package-to-dev workflow proceeds from the adopted checkout ...

AFTER (54b4ba80ab)
$ OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR=<private>/checkout openclaw update --channel dev --yes
Error: OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR already exists: <private>/checkout.
Package-to-dev conversion creates a fresh OpenClaw checkout and will not reuse existing directories.
Move it or set OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR to an unused path.

$ OPENCLAW_GIT_DIR=<private>/unused-checkout openclaw update --channel dev --yes
... git clone https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw.git <private>/unused-checkout ...
... fetch/build/global-link complete from the fresh, config-sanitized checkout ...
```

## Validation

- Rebasing completed cleanly onto `origin/main` at `7cde0ac8c0`.
- `git diff --check origin/main` is clean.
- Independent Codex review was repeated throughout the recovery design; findings covering dangling global links, premature service repair, config-rewritten follow-up fetches, retry safety, and token retirement were addressed before push.
- Repository tests are delegated to secretless hosted PR CI per the repository policy for fork code; check results are attached to this PR.

AI-assisted implementation and review; all final changes were inspected and revised against the repository's contributor and update-safety policies.

target.title: fix(doctor): preserve unparseable config instead of silently discarding it
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw doctor --fix` could silently destroy user config. In a home whose gateway had never started (no last-known-good promotion record), running `doctor --fix` on an unparseable `openclaw.json` declined recovery and wrote a stripped best-effort config — silently dropping the user's `gateway` and `models` sections — then exited 0, implying success.

## Why This Change Was Made

`recoverConfigFromLastKnownGood` returns false with no promotion record (promotion only happens on gateway startup), so doctor fell through to writing a gutted config without preserving the original. The promoted-recovery path already preserves the corrupt file as `.clobbered.*`; the never-promoted path did not. Now, when the config is unparseable and unrecoverable, doctor preserves the original as `.clobbered.*` and refuses to apply repairs, exiting non-zero with the preserved path — never silently discarding user sections. Extracts a shared `preserveConfigSnapshotAsClobbered` helper; the working promoted-recovery path is unchanged.

## User Impact

A corrupt config on a fresh/never-started install is preserved and surfaced loudly instead of being silently gutted. No change to the already-correct recovery path when the gateway has run before.

## Evidence

- Regression test `doctor-config-preflight.test.ts`: never-promoted + unparseable + `--fix` → original preserved as `.clobbered.*` (identical SHA-256) and non-zero exit; the silent-strip behavior no longer occurs. 38+7 tests pass.
- Real CLI black-box: exit 1, warning contains the exact `.clobbered.*` path, current+preserved files byte-identical.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs` green on Testbox; autoreview clean.

target.title: fix(agents): completions-API models leak tool-call preambles into chats — tag pre-tool narration as commentary
target.body:
Closes #108945
Related: #25592, #80458

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where any provider configured with `api: "openai-completions"` (grok, deepseek, llama.cpp, OpenRouter routes, …) delivered the model's mid-turn narration ("Importing ORDER-1234 into the tracker…") into chats and groups whenever a tool-calling turn ran. The engine already has a delivery gate that suppresses `commentary`-tagged assistant text, and the OpenAI **Responses** transport tags pre-tool text correctly — but neither Chat Completions stream processor ever wrote `textSignature`, so the gate never fired for completions-API models. `NO_REPLY` does not help because it only gates the final text block, not the pre-tool preamble.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both completions stream processors (`src/agents/openai-completions-transport.ts` and `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.ts`) now participate in the same `textSignature` v1 tag→gate mechanism the Responses transport (`encodeTextSignatureV1`) and the Anthropic transport (`tagPendingCommentaryText`) already use. Addressing the review's P1 stream-ordering finding, the phase is resolved **before consumer-visible events**, not at stream end:

- **Provisional tagging at the tool-call boundary.** Both processors tag buffered narration as `commentary` immediately before the first tool-call event is emitted (native `tool_calls` and the DeepSeek DSML-recovered path), so `toolcall_start` partials and later snapshots never expose the text unphased.
- **Explicit rollback on the stripped-spurious path.** When tool calls arrive with `finish_reason: "stop"` and visible text (the processors drop them as spurious), `clearPendingCommentaryText` removes only the transport-generated `commentary-<n>` tags, so the legitimate text answer is delivered. A stream-end backstop re-tags tool turns whose narration arrived after the last tool call or that skipped streaming (message-shaped responses).
- **Embedded-subscriber withholding.** The subscriber already kept unphased Anthropic deltas out of durable block replies until the tool boundary resolves the phase; the same gate now covers `openai-completions`, closing the mid-drain/pre-tool-flush leak the review pointed at (`embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.messages.ts`).
- The Anthropic transport's `tagPendingCommentaryText` moved to `src/agents/transport-stream-shared.ts` (whose doc comment already states "Shared so every provider transport tags phases identically") and is reused by the completions transport.
- **No stored-data-model change:** `textSignature` is a long-standing optional field on persisted text blocks (already written by Responses/Anthropic transports); old transcripts remain valid, no migration is involved. The "serialized state" strings flagged in tests are fixture payloads.
- **Replay-safe:** completions request builders map assistant text blocks by `.text` only, so `textSignature` never reaches provider payloads.
- Non-goal: native Google/Vertex transports own a separate `textSignature` use (thought signatures) and are not part of this issue.

## User Impact

Users chatting with completions-API models no longer receive tool-call preambles as ordinary chat messages — neither in final replies nor via block/preview streaming mid-drain — while turns whose spurious tool calls are stripped still deliver their text answer. Progress-draft consumers (`streaming.progress.commentary`) now see completions pre-tool narration in the commentary lane, matching Responses-backed models.

## Evidence

Regression tests:

- Transport ordering: "tags pre-tool narration as commentary **before toolcall_start reaches consumers**" asserts the `toolcall_start` partial already carries the commentary signature; "keeps text untagged when spurious tool calls are stripped" covers the rollback (`openai-transport-stream.inline-reasoning-and-tool-calls.test-utils.ts`, mirrored for `packages/ai` in `openai-completions.test.ts`).
- Embedded subscriber: new `embedded-agent-subscribe.subscribe-embedded-agent-session.withholds-completions-pretool-narration.test.ts` covers (a) narration withheld from durable block replies on a `text_end` channel incl. the pre-tool buffer flush, (b) stripped-spurious turn still delivers its text, (c) plain non-tool answer delivers in full — the tool-use and stripped-spurious outcomes the review asked to cover.
- DeepSeek DSML shaping and buffered-text assertions updated to expect the tag (intended behavior change).

Validation (local, Linux, Node 22):

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/openai-transport-stream.test.ts    → 336 passed
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/anthropic-transport-stream.test.ts → 108 passed
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs embedded-agent-subscribe                      → 585 passed
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/ai                                   → 445 passed
pnpm tsgo && pnpm tsgo:test:src && pnpm tsgo:test:packages                → clean
pnpm deadcode:full                                                        → clean
```

### Live provider/channel run (redacted)

Isolated OpenClaw gateway built from this branch (separate `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`/`OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, loopback port), real OpenAI-compatible router provider (`api: "openai-completions"`, provider name redacted), model `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash`, real SSE streaming, webchat session driven via `gateway call chat.send`. Prompt asks the model to narrate before calling the `read` tool on a workspace file. Raw persisted transcript events (`transcript_events`, session store):

**Before — same scenario on `main` (a1ed5e7b3c): the pre-tool narration is an ordinary unphased text block, so every delivery surface treats it as a reply:**

```
seq 14 stopReason: toolUse model: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash
  [{"type":"text","text":"Сейчас прочитаю файл заказа..."},        ← no textSignature → delivered
   {"type":"toolCall","tool":"read"}]
seq 16 stopReason: stop
  [{"type":"text","text":"Заказ ORDER-1234: оплачен, …"}]           ← final reply
```

**After — this branch, identical prompt/provider: the transport tags the narration at the tool-call boundary; the engine's existing commentary gate routes it out of replies, and the final answer stays deliverable:**

```
seq 20 stopReason: toolUse model: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash
  [{"type":"text","text":"Сейчас прочитаю файл заказа...",
    "textSignature":"{\"v\":1,\"id\":\"commentary-0\",\"phase\":\"commentary\"}"},   ← suppressed
   {"type":"toolCall","tool":"read"}]
seq 22 stopReason: stop
  [{"type":"text","text":"Заказ ORDER-1234: оплачен, …"}]           ← final reply, unphased → delivered
```

**No over-suppression — ordinary no-tool turn on this branch delivers normally:**

```
stopReason: stop  [{"type":"text","text":"Париж."}]                  ← unphased → delivered
```


### Rendered Web UI output (Control UI webchat, this branch)

Playwright-driven Chromium against the isolated gateway's Control UI chat; text extracted from the rendered DOM (session-id sidebar cropped). The tool-calling turn renders as user message → tool-activity chip → final answer — **no pre-tool narration bubble**; a plain no-tool turn stays delivered:

```
Перед каждым вызовом инструмента обязательно пиши в чат одну короткую фразу…   You
Worked for 19s
Заказ ORDER-1234: оплачен, 42000 руб., доставка 18 июля.                        Assistant

Ответь одним предложением без использования инструментов: столица Франции?      You
Париж.                                                                          Assistant
```

(The model's narration surfaces only in the transient progress/commentary lane during the run, matching Responses-backed models; it never lands as a delivered reply bubble.)

The reproduced runs used the tool-calling prompt from the issue narrative ("Сейчас прочитаю файл заказа…" = "I will now read the order file…"). No credentials appear in the transcripts; provider hostname redacted.


Additional fixes from review round 2: the subscriber withholding gate now flushes permanently-phaseless completions text at `text_end` (before the event's own tail chunk, preserving prefix-before-suffix order) (the review\u2019s final-delivery regression; covered by "flushes withheld unphased text at text_end so ordinary answers stay deliverable"), and transcript redaction keeps the v1 commentary phase signature on completions/Anthropic routes so history-backed consumers cannot resurface suppressed narration (covered in `transcript-redact.test.ts`).

Round-3 updates: rebased onto current main (per review); `transcript-redact.ts` route classification split into `transcript-redact.routes.ts` to satisfy the max-lines gate the signature-allowlist change tripped.

Note on current CI: earlier failures were main-side breakage at the rebase base (`check-dependencies` unused exports; `check-test-types` via docs-sync export, fixed upstream in #109358) — the branch is now rebased past the fixes.

target.title: fix(agents): dripping proxy SSE bodies cancel via outer abort
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes concern that an OpenClaw proxy LLM SSE body can keep dripping after headers and reset per-chunk idle forever. Total stream lifetime must stay owned by the configured outer agent/provider abort budget (`signal`), not a hidden proxy-local ceiling.

Affected workflow: `streamProxy` (`/api/stream` SSE) when agents route model calls through a proxy server.

## Why This Change Was Made

`streamProxy` already bounds pre-header waits and per-chunk SSE idle (default 120s). After headers, the pre-header abort is intentionally cleared so `timeoutMs` is not an absolute stream deadline (#97235). Idle alone resets on every chunk.

ClawSweeper rejected an unconditional one-hour proxy-local default (`merge-risk: compatibility`) because whole-run budgets can exceed 1h. This revision:

1. Keeps total lifetime owned by `options.signal` / outer abort by default — **no proxy-local default ceiling**.
2. Keeps `streamDeadlineMs` as an **opt-in only** escape hatch for callers who explicitly want a proxy-local wall-clock.
3. Arms that opt-in deadline only after the response reader exists so `cancel()` can interrupt a drip.
4. Adds native loopback `/api/stream` proof for both outer abort and explicit `streamDeadlineMs`.

Non-goals: making pre-header `timeoutMs` an absolute stream deadline again; documenting a new one-hour product contract; live proxy provider auth.

## User Impact

Dripping keepalive-style proxy SSE bodies are canceled when the outer abort fires, without cutting off healthy streams that are still within a longer configured agent/provider budget. Callers that explicitly pass `streamDeadlineMs` get a bounded proxy-local wall-clock; everyone else keeps the prior lifetime ownership model.

## Evidence

Head: `7a5e2b27281`

### Exact commands

```bash
OPENCLAW_VITEST_MAX_WORKERS=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/runtime/proxy.test.ts
```

```text
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 6.22s
```

Includes:
- existing “pre-header timeout is not an absolute stream deadline” regression still green
- existing idle re-arm / idle stall regressions still green

- **native loopback** `/api/stream` drip canceled by outer `AbortSignal` → `stopReason: "aborted"`, `Request aborted by user`, elapsed < 1.5s
- **native loopback** `/api/stream` drip canceled by explicit `streamDeadlineMs: 250` → wall-clock error inside budget

```text
→ autoreview clean: no accepted/actionable findings reported
→ overall: patch is correct (0.95)
```

### Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: dripping SSE after headers cannot outlive the outer abort; opt-in deadline also works on native fetch/ReadableStream
- Environment: real Node `http` loopback on `127.0.0.1` + real `fetch` / SSE body (no mocked reader)

target.title: feat(config): add ordered config layers
target.body:
Related RFC: [RFC 0019: Managed Configuration](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/34)

## What problem this solves

Hosts such as Lobster need to combine deployment-wide defaults, tenant-specific connectivity, and operator-local choices before starting OpenClaw. Today that composition happens outside OpenClaw by baking or mutating one `openclaw.json`, so OpenClaw cannot validate the original documents or enforce the authority boundary that produced the effective config.

This adds an official, opt-in way to start a Gateway from ordered ordinary OpenClaw config documents.

## Why core support instead of `$include` or launcher-side merging

`$include` is useful for assembling one authored config document. It does not express that an earlier source owns a value, reject a later source that tries to replace it, prove that later tool policy only tightens the effective policy, or make the resulting runtime immutable.

A launcher can implement those rules itself, but then it must duplicate OpenClaw's JSON5/include/env/schema/plugin validation and OpenClaw sees only the flattened result. That is the baked-overlay problem this PR is intended to remove.

The core addition is deliberately narrow: one repeatable CLI option, one recursive composer, and one startup-only/read-only lifecycle. It adds no config keys and no host-, tenant-, or operator-specific roles.

## User impact

No behavior changes unless `--config-layer` is supplied. Regular config users do not encounter this feature.

Opted-in Gateways use the composed snapshot for their lifetime. Config-mutating RPCs and persistence paths targeting that Gateway's canonical config are rejected, and config hot reload is disabled. Writes for unrelated config paths remain allowed. Restart with new source documents to activate a change.

## Example

Lobster can materialize three normal OpenClaw config files:

```json5
// scout-global.json5
{
  gateway: { mode: "local" },
  tools: { deny: ["exec"] },
}
```

```json5
// tenant-network.json5
{
  gateway: {
    controlUi: {
      allowedOrigins: ["https://scout.example.tenant"],
    },
  },
  tools: { deny: ["exec", "web"] },
}
```

```json5
// operator-local.json5
{
  logging: { level: "debug" },
}
```

Then start OpenClaw explicitly:

```bash
openclaw gateway run \
  --config-layer global=./scout-global.json5 \
  --config-layer tenant=./tenant-network.json5 \
  --config-layer operator=./operator-local.json5
```

The labels could be `one`, `two`, and `three`; only declaration order matters.

## Delivered V1

- repeat `--config-layer <id=path>` in precedence order
- parse through OpenClaw JSON5, include, env, schema, and plugin validation
- compose sparse documents recursively
- keep earlier exact values authoritative
- allow later `tools.allow` / `tools.deny` values only when they provably tighten policy
- keep the composed runtime startup-only and read-only

target.title: feat(exec): deny-over-allow exec approval denylist (#6615)
target.body:
Fixes #6615. Supersedes #92456 (author inactive since 2026-06-12, no response to review, and conflicts with main). Full credit to @Hidetsugu55 for the STOP-list concept and dual-host enforcement direction retained here.

## Latest state — canonical owner and exact-head proof

- Exact PR head: `3a69fa8311d5261ddcae5bea1101e2570de50897`
- GitHub CI: **113/113 checks complete and green** on that head.
- Real Apple-silicon macOS proof, run and baseline-isolated by **@clawSean**: TS-Go core + core-test clean; all denylist feature paths green; **338 focused assertions passed**. Two unique pre-existing host-PATH tests are reported twice across Vitest projects and reproduce identically on `origin/main` (details below).
- `openclaw.json` `tools.exec.denylist` is now the **single persisted owner** of STOP rules. The earlier dual-persistence design was removed.

## What Problem This Solves

Exec approvals support allowlists, but operators cannot declare commands that must stop for explicit human review when the runtime is otherwise permissive (`security=full`, `ask=off`, broad allowlist, or durable trust). #6615 asks for a deny-over-allow layer so patterns such as `git push --force` cannot auto-run merely because another policy says “allow.”

## Design and implementation

### One canonical policy source

- Adds strict `tools.exec.denylist` configuration at the global and per-agent levels.
- `openclaw.json` is the only persisted owner of denylist rules.
- `exec-approvals.json` remains the approvals/allowlist store; it does not own or evaluate denylist policy.
- Stray legacy `denylist` keys in `exec-approvals.json` are tolerated on read, warned once, and stripped on rewrite. Protocol writes reject the removed field.
- This eliminates the mixed-version risk where an older approvals-file writer could silently erase the STOP list.

### Shared matching and deny-over-allow semantics

- Denylist entries reuse the existing exec glob matcher rather than introducing a second pattern language.
- Global and per-agent config layers are normalized, de-duplicated, and unioned: a deny anywhere wins.
- Exact commands, glob patterns, basename variants, resolved executable paths, and shell-wrapper inner payloads are screened.
- If a configured denylist cannot safely analyze a command, execution fails closed into approval rather than bypassing the STOP rule.
- `security=deny` remains the strongest policy. A denylist hit otherwise beats `security=full`, `ask=off`, allowlist matches, and durable `allow-always` trust.

### Gateway, node-host, and macOS companion enforcement

- Gateway-host exec screens the effective config denylist before allowlist/auto-run decisions.
- Node-host `system.run` evaluates the same config policy and returns `denylist-hit` when an unapproved match reaches the node.
- Caller-visible denylist hits enter the registered human approval path even at `security=full` / `ask=off`; model auto-review cannot clear a STOP rule.
- Explicit human allow-once can authorize that invocation, but a denylist-approved `allow-always` decision is downgraded to one-shot so it cannot mint durable trust.
- Approval-backed execution carries denylist provenance through the node/macOS companion boundary.

### Dispatch-time revocation and TOCTOU hardening

- Approval-backed commands bind a canonical execution plan rather than later mutable command/cwd/session input.
- The runtime re-reads the current config denylist immediately before dispatch. A STOP rule added while approval is pending revokes the stale authority.
- Revalidation covers local node execution and macOS companion delegation, including rules targeting the resolved executable path.
- The macOS companion revalidates forwarded denylist provenance inside its locked execution commit and suppresses persistent approval for denylisted runs.

## Behavior proof

Control command: `git push --force origin main`, already allowlisted and durably trusted at `security=full` / `ask=off`.

```text
WITHOUT tools.exec.denylist
gateway host -> AUTO-RUN
node host    -> ALLOWED

WITH tools.exec.denylist = [{ pattern: "git push*--force*", reason: "history rewrite" }]
gateway host -> HUMAN APPROVAL REQUIRED
node host    -> DENIED (denylist-hit) unless the registered human approval is supplied

AFTER explicit allow-once
node host    -> ALLOWED ONCE; no durable trust is created
```

Focused regression coverage also proves that a config STOP rule added while an approval is pending revokes dispatch, including the macOS companion path.

## Evidence

### GitHub CI — exact head

- Head: `3a69fa8311d5261ddcae5bea1101e2570de50897`
- **113 completed / 113 green / 0 pending / 0 failed**
- Includes Linux test matrices, generated-artifact checks, dependency/architecture checks, and `macos-swift`.

### Real macOS/arm64 — exact head (not CI)

Proof credit: **@clawSean** ran the exact-head Apple-silicon matrix and independently reproduced the two host-specific cases against `origin/main` to separate environmental behavior from the PR diff.

Environment: macOS 26.5.1 (build 25F80), Darwin 25.5.0, Apple silicon `arm64`; node `v24.16.0`; repo-pinned pnpm `11.2.2`; Vitest `4.1.9`; frozen install clean.

- `pnpm tsgo:core` — exit 0
- `pnpm tsgo:core:test` — exit 0
- `src/infra/exec-approvals-denylist.test.ts` — 19 passed
- `src/node-host/exec-policy.test.ts` — 16 passed
- `src/node-host/invoke-system-run.test.ts` — 81 passed
- `src/agents/bash-tools.exec-host-gateway.test.ts` — 80 passed per project
- `src/config/config.schema-regressions.test.ts` — 40 passed
- `src/config/schema.help.quality.test.ts` — 22 passed

Aggregate: **338 passed**. The run reports four failures, but they are two unique pre-existing environment tests duplicated under `agents-core` and `agents-support`:

1. `/var` vs `/private/var` temporary-path canonicalization (macOS system symlink).
2. `cd .` vs `/usr/bin/cd .` because macOS provides a PATH-resolvable `/usr/bin/cd`.

Both tests exist verbatim on `origin/main` at `ff8a0159`. Swapping the denylist source files for that baseline and rerunning the two cases reproduces them identically, proving they are host-environment behavior rather than PR regressions. Every denylist-specific assertion passes.

## Scope

- Config schema/types/help/docs; shared denylist evaluation and authorization helpers.
- Gateway exec host, node `system.run`, and macOS companion enforcement.
- Protocol validation, generated baselines, and focused regression tests.
- No unrelated behavior refactors and no second persisted policy owner.

target.title: fix(ollama): dripping model pulls hang past idle timeout during setup
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where OpenClaw Ollama setup could hang forever while downloading a model when `/api/pull` kept sending occasional NDJSON progress lines that never advanced `completed`.

Affected workflow: Ollama provider setup / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` model download.

## Why This Change Was Made

Ollama setup already aborts if headers never arrive (30s) and already fails if the pull stream goes fully idle (300s). After headers return, that response timer was cleared, so only the per-chunk idle timer remained. Idle resets on every chunk, so a slow drip can keep the download alive indefinitely.

This keeps the headers and byte-idle budgets as-is, then arms a **no-progress watchdog** after the first body chunk. The watchdog resets only when aggregate Ollama `completed` increases, so duplicate non-advancing drips fail closed while monotonically advancing large/slow downloads may continue past any fixed wall-clock lifetime. Optional `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs` / `streamIdleTimeoutMs` on `ensureOllamaModelPulled` are for tests only — no new config key or env var. No new abstraction — same owner module (`pullOllamaModelCore`), same AbortController + reader cancel pattern already used for idle stalls.

ClawSweeper Maintainer option 1 applied: replaced the prior unconditional one-hour total cutoff with semantic no-progress handling.

Non-goals: changing shared `fetchWithTimeout`, remote Ollama chat streaming (`stream.ts`), or adding a hard total lifetime cap.

**Collision check:** `path:extensions/ollama/src/setup.ts` open PRs = 0 for this timeout policy. Nearby open ollama PRs touch streaming/NDJSON elsewhere, not setup pull no-progress.

## User Impact

During Ollama setup, a wedged or maliciously dripping `/api/pull` stream (bytes without advancing `completed`) fails closed with a no-progress error instead of hanging the wizard forever. Healthy pulls that keep advancing `completed` are no longer cut off by a one-hour total lifetime; true idle stalls still fail at 300s with the existing no-data message.

## Evidence

### Behavior or issue addressed

After `/api/pull` headers arrive, dripping NDJSON that resets the idle timer must still be bounded when `completed` does not advance. Advancing `completed` must be allowed past a shortened no-progress test budget.

### Canonical reachability path

Setup wizard / `ensureOllamaModelPulled` → `pullOllamaModel` → `pullOllamaModelCore` → first body chunk arms no-progress → advancing `completed` re-arms → non-advancing drip → `reader.cancel()` → no-progress error → `WizardCancelledError`.

### Focused tests

Exact head: `bf6b4987916837b2712d510ff2ef382736331edb`

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama/src/setup.test.ts extensions/ollama/src/setup.pull-deadline.loopback.test.ts
```

```text
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  34 passed (34)
```

Coverage:
- existing idle-stall regression still green at 300s with **no data** message (empty body; no-progress not armed)
- fake-timer non-advancing drip (`streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 1000`, idle 10s) fails with no-progress message
- fake-timer advancing `completed` continues past several shortened no-progress windows and downloads successfully
- loopback negative control: drip every 40ms + idle 100ms stays unsettled at 500ms (idle alone insufficient)
- loopback positive control: non-advancing drip + `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 250` rejects with no-progress message
- loopback advancing control: `completed` advances every 80ms under `streamNoProgressTimeoutMs: 250` and finishes successfully past that budget

### Real environment / loopback proof

Node local Vitest + standalone `node:http` on `127.0.0.1` only:

- **Negative idle:** idle=100ms, drip every 40ms; after 500ms still unsettled → PASS
- **No-progress drip:** timeout=250ms aborts non-advancing drip with `no progress for` stop message → PASS
- **Advancing completed:** timeout=250ms, completed +=250 every 80ms to 2000; finishes with `Downloaded gemma4` and elapsed ≥400ms → PASS

### Diff hygiene

Live `ollama.com` / LAN Ollama daemon multi-hour large-model pull; controlled local drip + advancing `completed` only.

### Risk / Compatibility

Low. Removes the previous unconditional one-hour total cutoff (compatibility-preserving vs that draft). Retains headers + byte-idle. Adds semantic no-progress aligned with idle budget (300s default). Test-only timeout overrides only (no new config/env). Intentional fail-closed for indefinitely non-advancing drips.

target.title: fix(agents): add global thinkingDefault fallback in resolveAgentConfig (#109276)
target.body:
Closes #109276

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who set `agents.defaults.thinkingDefault` in their `openclaw.json` config would see no effect — thinking blocks never appeared in session history for any agent that had a `list` entry without an explicit per-agent `thinkingDefault` override. The global default was silently ignored, requiring users to set `thinkingDefault` on every agent entry individually.

This was discovered while investigating why Ollama Cloud models (such as `glm-5.2:cloud`, `deepseek-v4-pro:cloud`) never produced thinking blocks. The Ollama API, stream parser, and persistence pipeline all work correctly when thinking is enabled — the root cause was that the configured thinking level never reached the stream wrapper.

## Why This Change Was Made

In `resolveAgentConfig()` (`src/agents/agent-scope-config.ts:135`), `thinkingDefault` was read directly from the per-agent entry with no nullish coalescing fallback to `agentDefaults?.thinkingDefault`. The very next line for `verboseDefault` (line 136) and a few lines below for `contextTokens` (line 139) both correctly include `?? agentDefaults?.xxx` fallback. This was an unintentional omission introduced when the `verboseDefault` fallback was added in commit `3599ab2e56` — `thinkingDefault` was left behind.

The fix applies the same `?? agentDefaults?.thinkingDefault` pattern, making `resolveAgentConfig` consistent with its own established merge logic and with the documented resolution order (per-agent default > global default).

Scope is limited to the resolver-level inheritance defect. No other fields are changed.

## User Impact

Users who set `agents.defaults.thinkingDefault` globally can now rely on it taking effect for all agents in their `agents.list[]`, without needing to duplicate the value on every entry. The config example below now works as documented:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "thinkingDefault": "high"
    },
    "list": [
```
