target.title: feat: add readiness conditions and providers
target.body:
Related RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/33

## Problem

OpenClaw already exposes Gateway `/ready` and `/readyz`, but readiness is evaluated by a fixed set of Gateway checks. Hosts and operators cannot select the additional criteria that define readiness for a deployment, plugins cannot contribute bounded observational evidence, and CLI, health, and status surfaces do not share one canonical result.

That leaves Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, OCC, and other hosts maintaining private scripts to answer a basic question: is this OpenClaw instance ready to accept work under its configured requirements?

## Proposal

This PR implements the readiness portion of RFC 0018:

- normalize Gateway startup, admission, drain, selected-channel, suppressed-channel, event-loop, configuration, plugin, and workspace evidence into structured conditions
- distinguish required conditions, which fail readiness on `False` or `Unknown`, from advisory conditions, which remain visible without changing the ready result
- let operators select built-in and plugin-contributed criteria directly with `gateway.readiness`
- let activated plugins register namespaced, self-describing criteria through the public plugin registry
- bound plugin checks with per-criterion timeouts, an overall readiness deadline, stable redacted timeout/error results, short caching, and in-flight coalescing that never duplicates a callback still pending after timeout
- return a required `ReadinessEvaluationComplete=Unknown` condition if canonical evaluation times out or fails, rather than hanging or rejecting health/status requests
- project the same canonical result through `/ready`, `/readyz`, Gateway `ready`, health, status, and `openclaw ready`
- provide human-readable and `--json` CLI output with fail-closed exit status

Example operator selection:

```json5
{
  gateway: {
    readiness: {
      requiredCriteria: ["openclaw.workspace-writable", "plugin.example.dependency"],
      advisoryCriteria: ["plugin.metrics.exporter"],
    },
  },
}
```

Core selector IDs are configuration identities: selecting `openclaw.workspace-writable` emits the stable canonical `WorkspaceWritable` condition. Plugin criteria use their full namespaced ID as the condition type.

A plugin may contribute observational evidence without changing readiness by default:

```ts
api.registerReadinessCriterion({
  id: "dependency",
  description: "Example dependency is reachable",
  async check({ pluginConfig, signal }) {
    const reachable = await probeDependency(pluginConfig, { signal });
    return reachable
      ? { status: "True", reason: "DependencyReachable", message: "Dependency is reachable." }
      : { status: "False", reason: "DependencyUnavailable", message: "Dependency is unavailable." };
  },
});
```

Core publishes that registration as `plugin.<plugin-id>.dependency`. Operators explicitly select it in `requiredCriteria` when it belongs in their serving contract.

## Compatibility

Existing `/ready` and `/readyz` routes retain their HTTP contract: `200` when all required conditions are true and `503` otherwise. Existing installations need no readiness configuration. The universal Gateway lifecycle baseline always applies; explicitly selected criteria add deployment-specific evidence.

This PR does **not** add hosting profiles, profile selection, node-mode profiles, runtime activation identity, release conformance, Lobster concepts, tenant concepts, OCC resources, or policy/Doctor dependencies. Standard Hosting Profiles are separated into RFC 0023 so this readiness facility can stand on its own.

## Review Stack

This is one upstream PR with four commits. The fork PRs preserve the same smaller review boundaries:

- [PR 17: canonical Gateway readiness conditions](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/17)
- [PR 22: workspace writability criterion](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/22)
- [PR 23: selectable readiness providers](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/23)
- [PR 27: canonical `openclaw ready` CLI](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/27)

The implementation is rebased onto OpenClaw main `4e78d91c0f96`.

## Validation

- exact head: `17b34f792d87da05ff1b4d1e99587f96f08e0dde`
- all 19 changed test files pass across eight selected Vitest project shards and 211 assertions
- Oxfmt passes on 59 changed TypeScript/JavaScript/Markdown files; Oxlint passes on 54 changed TypeScript/JavaScript files; `git diff --check` passes
- plugin SDK surface validation passes at the exact post-harvest budget: 328 public entrypoints and 10,615 public exports, with no forbidden package subpaths
- package build, public SDK declaration graph, package inventory, and tarball integrity checks pass
- ClawSweeper found the pre-rebase patch correct; this exact-head rebase removes the requested changelog entry and passes the source, SDK, and build gates below
- package-installed Docker proof on patch-equivalent head `89d8607aab9f` passes with image `sha256:8add3c4f8ce2f1a444a735c43f19eac4ee0212778123fb883ff8f9f785a9fd0d`
- `/ready` and `/readyz` transition `200 -> 503 -> 200` when a required workspace is removed and restored; `/healthz` remains `200`; `openclaw ready --json` exits `0 -> 1 -> 0` with the same `WorkspaceWritable / WorkspaceMissing` condition

`pnpm check:changed` is not claimed locally: this linked WSL worktree delegates that command to Blacksmith Testbox, and the local credential cannot access the `openclaw` organization. The changed-file tests and local static/package gates above passed; GitHub CI remains authoritative for repository-wide lanes.

## Published Upgrade Proof

The repository's `published-upgrade-survivor` Docker lane passed from the current published `openclaw@2026.7.1` package to a `2026.7.2` tarball carrying this four-commit readiness patch.

```text
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_PUBLISHED_BASELINE=1 \
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_BASELINE_SPEC=openclaw@2026.7.1 \
OPENCLAW_UPGRADE_SURVIVOR_CANDIDATE=current \
NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=16384 \
  bash scripts/e2e/upgrade-survivor-docker.sh
```

The lane installed and configured 2026.7.1 first, seeded agents, sessions, workspaces, credentials, channel/plugin settings, and legacy plugin dependency state, validated the baseline, upgraded the same installation through `openclaw update`, ran non-interactive Doctor and config validation, and revalidated preserved state before starting the candidate Gateway.

All 54 recorded phases passed on proved head `e5f5e97332e5495e65c1993dba258109849bdece`. Gateway startup took 47 seconds, `/healthz` 1 second, `/readyz` 1 second, and RPC status 2 seconds. The current head is rebased onto `4e78d91c0f96`. It preserves the four readiness commits, removes the release-owned changelog line requested by review, adapts the shared Gateway request-context type to current main, and refreshes the intentional Plugin SDK budgets and API baseline. Exact-head changed tests, formatting, lint, SDK checks, and the full package build pass; the package-installed Docker and published-upgrade results above remain the immediately preceding runtime compatibility evidence.

Compatibility is explicit: the upgraded existing installation did not silently acquire `WorkspaceWritable` or another opt-in criterion as a new requirement. Its existing Gateway lifecycle baseline remained ready. An operator who explicitly requires workspace writability receives the intended fail-closed transition and matching CLI exit status.

target.title: refactor(plugin-sdk): isolate core session state from plugin mutations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an isolation gap where core-owned restart-recovery coordination could be exposed, overwritten, or lost through Plugin SDK session APIs.

Upstream now persists channel-turn recovery fields under the `restartRecovery*` namespace. This PR keeps those shipped fields, as well as the later split series' `mainRestartRecovery` aggregate, out of plugin reads, callback inputs, replacements, ACP resolution, and injected runtime surfaces.

The repair also addresses two earlier review findings: an identity-preserving whole-store key move could silently drop private recovery state, and the ACP SDK declared that it returned the internal `AcpSessionManager` class even though the runtime object was already a restricted facade.

## Why This Change Was Made

Plugin-visible session rows now pass through one projection/reconciliation owner. The public `SessionEntry` type omits `mainRestartRecovery` and the complete `restartRecovery*` namespace, matching runtime behavior.

Private recovery state is retained for same-key updates and for a unique one-to-one `sessionId` key move. It is not copied when the source or destination mapping is ambiguous, and it is cleared when the effective session identity changes. Future `restartRecovery*` plugin extension slots are reserved before a new core field can collide with them.

The ACP getter returns an explicit `AcpSessionManagerFacade` interface. The runtime object remains stable, frozen, null-prototype, and limited to bound public methods, so plugins cannot reach the internal manager constructor or bypass session projection.

Compatibility note: released `v2026.7.1-beta.5` / `v2026.7.1` and the frozen PR #96230 returned the real manager class. This PR intentionally does not preserve `instanceof`, prototype, or constructor identity because exposing the internal constructor would reopen the private-session-state escape path. The SDK catalog documents that contract for maintainer review.

## User Impact

Plugin authors continue to use the same session and ACP methods, while current and future core restart-recovery coordination remains private and survives valid session-key moves.

Plugins that relied on `getAcpSessionManager()` being an actual internal class instance must migrate to the structural `AcpSessionManagerFacade` contract. No session schema, storage format, ACP method behavior, retry budget, or production `mainRestartRecovery` writer is added by this PR.

## Evidence

- Recovery isolation matrix: 9 files, 82/82 tests passed across direct Plugin SDK APIs, modern and deprecated whole-store mutation, unique and ambiguous key moves, ACP, agent runtime, channel runtime, combined transcript-store reads, injection rejection, and session identity rotation.
- Plugin SDK surface budget tests: 10/10 passed.
- Public API contract: generated declarations expose the projected `SessionEntry` and `AcpSessionManagerFacade`; no `mainRestartRecovery` or `restartRecovery*` declaration remains in the generated SDK baseline.
- Plugin SDK API baseline, public export budget, formatting, lint, max-lines ratchet, and diff-check passed after syncing to exact base `ff1687e04f11df6c35002c4531cdafba6a845f8f`.
- Upstream's current public Plugin SDK export baseline is 7,991; this PR's reviewed `AcpSessionManagerFacade` is the sole additional export, for a passing budget of 7,992.
- Source audit found no remaining critical, major, minor, security, performance, persistence, or public-contract issue.
- Frozen PR comparison at `edc24088387a8d573798233979a71f3b40a24ac9` confirms that its whole-store implementation lacked cross-key recovery transfer and its ACP SDK returned the internal class directly.
- The branch contains zero production `mainRestartRecovery` producers. Existing upstream `restartRecovery*` writers remain unchanged and now sit behind the Plugin SDK projection boundary.
- Range-diff against the prior reviewed PR2 head found the five functional commits patch-equivalent; the resync changed only upstream surface-budget context and the generated API hash.

Protected local TypeScript validation could not be recorded because this machine cannot attest the required cgroup limits; the guard stopped before execution and was not bypassed. GitHub CI remains the authoritative protected typecheck/build lane.

Per maintainer-requested workflow for this split, the final audit is a complete code-diff/source review rather than a separate automated final-review pass.

target.title: fix(codex): bound app-server websocket handshake waits to requestTimeoutMs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using Codex app-server over websocket/unix transport would hang forever on initialize/RPC when a peer accepted the socket but never completed the WebSocket upgrade.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bound upgrades with `ws.handshakeTimeout` **and** an explicit CONNECTING deadline at the transport chokepoint (`createWebSocketTransport`). `ws.handshakeTimeout` alone does **not** abort custom `createConnection` (Unix) upgrades — verified with a never-upgrade peer that stayed CONNECTING past the library timeout.

Production budget is resolved `appServer.requestTimeoutMs` (default 60s) from `CodexAppServerClient.start` via `resolveCodexAppServerRuntimeOptions()`.

**CI / landing notes**
- Touching `transport-websocket.ts` triggers full CodeQL `network-runtime-boundary`, which currently fails on main's unclassified `openApnsTlsTunnel` `tls.connect`. This head includes that allowlist so CI can pass; preferred split remains [#109357](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109357).
- Also includes the missing `pruneOrphanLocaleDocs` typings export so `check:test-types` is not blocked by current main debt (same fix as [#109364](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109364)).

Collision check: [#108795](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/108795) closed unmerged; APNs allowlist split candidate [#109357](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109357); typings unblocker [#109364](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109364).

## User Impact

- **Before:** never-upgrade peers hang initialize/RPC forever (TCP and Unix).
- **After:** handshake follows operator `requestTimeoutMs` (default 60s) on both TCP and Unix, then emits transport exit (`1006`).

## Evidence

Exact head: `f4fc148cf5f69f456f5df0ca14f262d09720b1cf`

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/transport-websocket.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

target.title: feat: add standard hosting profiles
target.body:
Related RFC: https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/37

Depends on: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104018

> **Stacked implementation:** this branch contains exact readiness head `17b34f792d8` from PR 104018 followed by nine profile-only commits. Until PR 104018 lands, GitHub's aggregate diff against `main` includes both layers. After it lands, this PR reduces to the Hosting Profiles work described below.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw runs locally, in containers, behind identity proxies, and as a controller for paired execution targets, but those deployment labels are not reproducible support contracts. Operators currently spread the intended posture across startup flags, environment, config, container probes, adapter code, and private checklists. A Gateway process can be alive and logging while it still cannot safely serve its intended workload.

This change makes that distinction explicit. A selected profile names the posture OpenClaw is expected to satisfy, and the canonical readiness result remains `503` with stable reasons until every required runtime fact is true.

## Standard Hosting Profiles

Profiles are named, release-tested presets over the canonical readiness conditions from PR 104018. They do not introduce a second health system.

| Profile | Supported posture | Additional required readiness evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | Explicit foreground or local Gateway posture | Universal Gateway readiness and writable workspace |
| `container` | Directly reachable container listener | Non-loopback effective listener and writable mounted workspace |
| `reverse-proxy` | Gateway behind a trusted identity proxy | Trusted-proxy auth mode, identity header, trusted source, and writable workspace |
| `node-mode` | Gateway controlling one or more execution targets | Approved pairing, connected target, approved command surface, live control channel, and writable workspace |

Profiles are opt-in. Without a selected profile, OpenClaw preserves the readiness baseline from PR 104018 and does not silently add profile conditions. When selected, precedence is:

```text
gateway startup argument > environment > openclaw.json
```

Operators select a profile through `hosting.profile`, `OPENCLAW_HOSTING_PROFILE`, or `gateway run --hosting-profile`. Invalid startup values fail before destructive runtime reset/force behavior. Results include a logical runtime ID and a unique process/container incarnation ID.

Profiles validate effective runtime state. They do not generate or repair configuration, encode scheduler retry policy, introduce Lobster/OCC concepts, or replace direct readiness-condition selection.

## Why This Helps Operators

Docker, Kubernetes, systemd, OCC, and downstream hosts can consume the ordinary `/readyz` contract instead of reconstructing readiness from logs or process liveness. A host receives `200` only when the selected posture can serve work; expected deployment failures return `503` and a named condition explaining what remains unmet.

This matters most for partial startup. For example, node-mode remains non-ready when its Gateway is running, and remains non-ready even after a node transport connects, until the node command surface is explicitly approved. The host does not send traffic merely because a process exists.

Maintainers gain a bounded support matrix for reproducing deployment issues against a named posture rather than an open-ended configuration claim.

## Implementation Stack

Readiness dependency head: `17b34f792d8`

Profile-only commits:

1. `642bed18093` standard `local`, `container`, and `reverse-proxy` profiles
2. `b9121934a7f` product-neutral `node-mode` readiness
3. `2b10b218279` runtime activation identity
4. `81f787820da` packaged profile conformance and release wiring
5. `05bbe94f8d5` startup validation and lifecycle safety
6. `ab612666315` host-provisioned workspace proof
7. `630684819c8` explicit node approval readiness proof
8. `f54affa3983` explicit opt-in activation and upgrade-safe unprofiled proof
9. `672bc488cfd` discoverable Hosting Profiles operator documentation

Profile-only diff: 34 files, 1,452 insertions, and 5 deletions, including docs and tests.

Fork review slices: [#18](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/18), [#19](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/19), [#42](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/42), and [#21](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/21). [Fork PR #94](https://github.com/giodl73-repo/openclaw/pull/94) preserves the profile-only diff against the readiness branch.

## Verification

Current head: `672bc488cfdcd798763b943babb136793a6efb0b`.

Runtime implementation and Docker proof head: `f54affa3983b4803e424e098cf1b359c42481704`. The final commit adds only the Hosting Profiles guide, configuration reference, CLI cross-link, and docs navigation.

Environment: isolated Ubuntu 24.04 checkout, Node 24.15+, Docker Linux/amd64. No Lobster, OCC, tenant service, or unpublished local dependency was involved.

Focused source verification:

- 273 focused assertions passed across the changed profile, runtime, node-mode, config, CLI, planner, release, Gateway startup, and readiness files.
- The profile-added `gateway.test.ts` startup assertion passes alone. In the broad file, the unrelated `sessions.abort` timeout reproduces on the exact readiness base; the workspace-plugin count assertion is order-sensitive and passes when selected directly on both heads.
- Shell syntax, JavaScript syntax, Oxfmt on 30 files, Oxlint on 26 files, and `git diff --check` pass.
- Codex review of the eight runtime profile commits against readiness head `17b34f792d8` found no actionable correctness regression.
- The docs-only tip passes `pnpm docs:list`, Oxfmt, JSON parsing for `docs/docs.json`, and `git diff --check`.

target.body:
## Summary

Implements the first read-only slice of [RFC #27](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27) behind `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`:

- Defines the strict grouped Claw v1 schema for one new agent plus its workspace files, packages, MCP servers, and cron jobs.
- Enforces portable exact SemVer, canonical ClawHub names, cross-platform workspace paths, managed avatars, five-field timezone-qualified cron schedules, pinned package-manager MCP commands, safe spawn environment keys, and HTTPS/loopback remote MCP URLs.
- Reads local package or standalone sources into a deterministic development snapshot that binds the manifest, package metadata, and every referenced workspace source.
- Produces a complete read-only add plan with expected state, stable diagnostics, local readiness requirements, and a `planIntegrity` digest that later mutation must bind to explicit consent.
- Blocks agent, workspace, MCP, cron, and unsafe source collisions instead of merging into an existing agent.
- Exposes only `openclaw claws inspect <source>` and `openclaw claws add <source> --dry-run`; without the process opt-in, `claws` is absent from registration and help.

This PR does not mutate config or disk, run package installers, configure MCP, create cron jobs, or persist provenance. Package actions remain explicit blockers until the package-owner lifecycle slice later in the stack.

## Stack

- RFC: [openclaw/rfcs#27](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27)
- This PR: schema, source identity, diagnostics, readiness, and read-only planning
- Next: [#101755](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101755) creates the new agent/workspace and root provenance record

## Validation

`resolveInitialCronDelivery` in `src/cron/service/initial-delivery.ts` only checks `sessionTarget === "isolated"` when deciding whether to inject default `{ mode: "announce" }` delivery. target.title: fix(agents): do not label finish_reason error as LLM timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When OpenRouter (or Google via OpenRouter) finishes a stream quickly with `finish_reason: "error"`, OpenClaw classified that completed provider failure as a timeout. Operators saw **LLM request timed out.** with `failoverReason: timeout` / 408-class signaling, even when `durationMs` was only a few seconds and `rawErrorPreview` was `Provider finish_reason: error`. That sends people to timeout/network knobs that cannot fix a provider-completed error. Model fallback still ran; the bug is mislabeling and bad diagnostics.

## Evidence

Production classifier modules on this branch (not a copied mock):

```console
$ pnpm exec tsx scripts/proof-finish-reason-error-not-timeout.mjs
BEFORE contract (expected failure modes without the fix):
  finish_reason:error matched ERROR_PATTERNS.timeout → reason=timeout, copy=LLM request timed out.

AFTER (production modules on this branch):
  {"sample":"Provider finish_reason: error","reason":"server_error","isTimeout":false,"isProvider":true}
  {"sample":"finish_reason: error","reason":"server_error","isTimeout":false,"isProvider":true}
  {"sample":"stop reason: error","reason":"server_error","isTimeout":false,"isProvider":true}
  {"sample":"Unhandled stop reason: error","reason":"server_error","isTimeout":false,"isProvider":true}
  {"sample":"Provider finish_reason: network_error","reason":"timeout","isTimeout":true,"isProvider":false}
  {"sample":"Provider finish_reason: abort","reason":"timeout","isTimeout":true,"isProvider":false}
  {"sample":"Provider finish_reason: malformed_response","reason":"timeout","isTimeout":true,"isProvider":false}
  userFacing="Provider finish_reason: error"

RESULT: PASS — bare finish_reason:error is server_error, not timeout
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Bare `finish_reason: error` / stop-reason `error` was matched by `ERROR_PATTERNS.timeout`, rewritten to "LLM request timed out.", and classified as timeout/408 even for fast provider-completed failures (issue #109218).
- **Real environment tested:** macOS 15, Node v26.5.0, worktree `/tmp/oc-109218` on branch `fix/finish-reason-error-not-timeout` rebased onto latest `upstream/main`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

  ```bash
  cd /tmp/oc-109218
  pnpm exec tsx scripts/proof-finish-reason-error-not-timeout.mjs
  ```

- **Evidence after fix:** terminal output under Evidence. Production `classifyFailoverReason` / `isTimeoutErrorMessage` / `formatAssistantErrorText` return `server_error`, not timeout, and keep the provider finish_reason string for operators. Abort/network/malformed finish reasons stay in the timeout lane.
- **Observed result after fix:** Provider-completed bare `error` finish/stop reasons are failover-eligible `server_error` with accurate user-facing copy; genuine transport hangs and network finish reasons remain timeouts.
- **What was not tested:** Live OpenRouter stream against a real key (no credentials in this environment). The production classifiers are the same functions the gateway uses on the agent-end error path.

## Summary

Closes #109218.

Remove bare `error` from timeout stop/finish patterns; add `isProviderCompletedErrorFinishReasonMessage` and classify as `server_error` before the timeout rewrite in `formatAssistantErrorText` and sanitize. Keep abort / network_error / malformed_response as timeout-like for #61281.

target.title: fix(secrets): keep startup alive when TTS SecretRefs are missing
target.body:
<!-- submission-timestamps:start -->
First submitted: July 6, 2026, 10:00 PM (US Eastern Time) / 02:00 UTC.
Last body edit: July 15, 2026, 3:56 AM (US Eastern Time) / 07:56 UTC.
Latest head commit: July 15, 2026, 3:47 AM (US Eastern Time) / 07:47 UTC.
<!-- submission-timestamps:end -->

Closes #101204

## What Problem This Solves

A configured but temporarily missing built-in TTS API-key SecretRef currently aborts Gateway startup and takes unrelated chat, auth, tools, channels, and plugins offline even though only speech synthesis needs that credential. This PR keeps the first activating startup available while preserving strict failure for every non-activating, reload, restart-check, config-write, malformed-ref, policy, provider, contract, mismatch, and invalid-value path.

## Summary

A missing built-in TTS provider API-key SecretRef no longer aborts an otherwise healthy Gateway during the first activating startup. The affected TTS provider remains unconfigured, startup emits a structured warning, and unrelated chat, auth, tools, channels, and plugins continue to start.

The exception is deliberately narrow. It requires all of the following:

- the lifecycle reason is `startup`;
- the operation will activate the prepared snapshot (`activate === true`);
- no active secrets runtime snapshot exists;
- the assignment is a built-in TTS provider API key explicitly marked optional; and
- resolution failed with the matching missing-value error for that exact ref.

Non-activating startup preparation, restart checks, reloads, config-write preflight, malformed refs, policy/security failures, provider failures, contract failures, mismatched errors, and invalid resolved value shapes remain fail-closed.

## Breaking changes

There is no config-shape, RPC, persistence, package, or dependency change. Failure timing changes for one credential class: a missing built-in TTS API-key SecretRef is reported as a startup warning and fails locally when that TTS provider is used, rather than aborting the entire first activating Gateway startup.

## Why / user impact

Built-in TTS is an optional capability, but SecretRef activation previously treated its API keys as credentials required by the whole Gateway. Operators may now keep an optional ElevenLabs or other built-in TTS SecretRef configured while its value is temporarily absent. The provider remains unavailable until the ref resolves, while unrelated Gateway capabilities stay online.

The stricter sibling paths are unchanged: reload, restart-check, non-activating startup preparation, and config-write preflight reject the unresolved ref and preserve the last-known-good runtime/config.

## Implementation

- `src/gateway/server-startup-config.ts` owns the lifecycle gate. Optional missing-value degradation is enabled only for `reason === "startup"`, `activate === true`, and an absent active runtime snapshot.
- The lifecycle gate is layered onto the current mainline `resolveGatewayStartupSecretProjection` contract. `sourceConfig` remains the recoverable full source, while an `assignmentConfig` may suppress unsafe channel assignments during crash-loop recovery; this PR does not collapse those responsibilities back into one pruned config.
- `src/secrets/runtime-config-collectors-tts.ts` marks only built-in TTS provider API-key assignments as optional at startup.
- `src/secrets/resolve-errors.ts` owns typed provider/ref errors and the exact missing-value classifier; `src/secrets/resolve.ts` assigns those codes at env/file/exec and provider-contract boundaries.
- `src/secrets/runtime-optional-assignments.ts` owns required/optional partitioning, independent optional resolution, warning emission, and redaction registration.
- `src/secrets/runtime-prepare.runtime.ts` exports that helper through the existing lazy startup facade, so the Gateway hot path does not statically load the full resolver.
- `src/secrets/runtime.ts` delegates assignment resolution once and remains focused on snapshot preparation/activation.
- `src/secrets/runtime-shared.ts` carries optional-assignment metadata while retaining existing resolved-value shape validation.

## Code-path analysis

- Runtime entry: `src/gateway/server-startup-config.ts` prepares secrets before Gateway startup activation.
- Lifecycle owner: `createRuntimeSecretsActivator` decides whether preparation is activating and whether a prior runtime snapshot exists.
- Mainline projection boundary: `src/gateway/server-startup-secret-surfaces.ts` separates recoverable source config from the assignment projection used during crash-loop recovery.
- Snapshot owner: `src/secrets/runtime.ts` prepares and activates the runtime snapshot.
- Optional-assignment owner: `src/secrets/runtime-optional-assignments.ts` resolves optional refs independently without weakening the required batch.
- Collector/caller: `src/secrets/runtime-config-collectors.ts` routes core/channel/plugin surfaces; `src/secrets/runtime-config-collectors-tts.ts` collects top-level, agent, and channel voice TTS API keys.
- Resolver/callee: `src/secrets/resolve.ts` resolves env/file/exec refs; `src/secrets/resolve-errors.ts` distinguishes absence from policy, validation, provider, and contract failures.
- Sibling invariant: Gateway auth, model/provider, plugin, channel-token, auth-store, and all other required assignments remain fail-closed.
- Localized runtime failure: `src/gateway/server-methods/tts.ts` returns the normal provider-not-configured `UNAVAILABLE` path when the degraded provider is selected.
- Adjacent coverage: `src/secrets/resolve.test.ts`, `src/secrets/runtime.test.ts`, `src/secrets/runtime-config-collectors-tts.test.ts`, `src/secrets/runtime-discord-surface.test.ts`, `src/gateway/server-startup-config.secrets.test.ts`, `src/gateway/server-methods/config.shared-auth.test.ts`, and `src/gateway/server-methods/tts.test.ts`.

## Mainline comparison

Rebased onto `OpenClaw/OpenClaw:main@4f71a2855e538185d16e7b04d3acc7f2f02a3944` (commit time 2026-07-15T07:43:03Z; fetched 2026-07-15T07:47Z).

Recent same-area mainline work was incorporated rather than overwritten:

- `701d02f241` made the Gateway startup secret-assignment projection explicit.
- `1eec68a6a0` preserved safe-mode secret recovery when suppressed channel secrets are unavailable.
- `3616fba951` made hot reload transactional.

The final rebase increment through `4f71a2855e` changed unrelated auto-reply tests, status formatting, signed-merge handling, Codex restricted-turn shell behavior, and Telegram archive fixtures. During the final exact-head proof, official `main` advanced through `1fe3a5f557` with plugin compatibility, terminal quoting, Codex adapter, and Testbox path changes; the GitHub compare contains no changes under this PR's startup lifecycle gate, `src/secrets/`, or TTS docs/tests.

## Branch / base provenance

- Base: `OpenClaw/OpenClaw:main@4f71a2855e538185d16e7b04d3acc7f2f02a3944`
- Head: `snowzlmbot/OpenClaw:fix/optional-tts-secret-startup@9a4986f4c3bafd96c69568794e522060c3e0608c`
- Evidence branch: `snowzlmbot/OpenClaw:proof/issue-101204-live@5c712d5c05475d5984ce73b36309202d2c367896`

- `Allow edits by maintainers` remains enabled.

## Dependency / contract verification

No dependency, lockfile, package, protocol, persisted schema, database, sidecar, or config-schema changes are included. The resolver error code is internal runtime classification used to preserve the existing fail-closed contract except for the explicitly optional, missing-value-only, first-activation TTS case.

No migration or upgrade compatibility step is required. Tests that serialize fixture configs or exercise the runtime cache do not alter a persisted data model.

## Labels considered

Observed automated labels include `gateway`, `docs`, compatibility risk, and security-boundary risk. No contributor-side label mutation was performed. The compatibility and security labels remain appropriate because the PR deliberately changes startup behavior for one credential class inside the shared secrets runtime.

## Validation

- `git diff --check` — passed on the current head.
- [Exact-head focused tests and live Gateway/RPC proof](https://github.com/snowzlmbot/openclaw/actions/runs/29398667816) — passed on evidence head `5c712d5c05475d5984ce73b36309202d2c367896`, whose direct parent is code head `9a4986f4c3bafd96c69568794e522060c3e0608c`. The run passed 90 focused tests, started a real Gateway with the missing TTS ref, observed the structured warning, and verified localized `tts.speak` failure while the Gateway stayed available.
- [Full upstream CI on the byte-equivalent rebased patch](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29397794848) — passed: 45 jobs successful and 11 skipped on `8e7cfaf489ec194bdb160bfcb881d8a55bb267d6`. The final rebase only advanced across unrelated mainline commits; stable patch-id for the complete PR diff remained `eec8e924514251d650ca5a89d501be1517bcd1b7`.
- Exact-current-head PR gates passed for CodeQL Critical Quality, OpenGrep PR diff, Workflow Sanity, Security Sensitive Guard, Dependency Guard, and the upstream Real behavior proof dispatcher. The current full CI and CodeQL runs remain linked in the PR check rollup.

## Evidence source map

[Evidence workflow run](https://github.com/snowzlmbot/openclaw/actions/runs/29398667816)

- Purpose: focused resolver/runtime/TTS collector/Discord voice/Gateway startup/TTS handler regression suite plus live Gateway/RPC behavior.

## Sanitized logs

```text
Tests       33 passed (33)
Test Files  4 passed (4)

Gateway started with missing optional ELEVENLABS_API_KEY SecretRef.
```

## Media evidence

target.title: Bound HTTP error body snippets to readable streams
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readResponseBodySnippet` was meant to produce a bounded diagnostic snippet for upstream HTTP error responses, but its body-less fallback used whole-body response methods before truncating. A response without a usable `ReadableStream.getReader()` could still force the process to materialize the entire error body just to produce a short snippet.

## Why This Change Was Made

This keeps the streamed path on `readResponseTextPrefix`, which already enforces the byte cap and cancels overflow, and fails closed for body-less/non-readable responses by returning an empty snippet instead of calling `text()` or `arrayBuffer()`. Without a readable stream there is no cancellable bounded prefix reader, so skipping the diagnostic body is safer than whole-body buffering.

## User Impact

Oversized upstream error bodies can no longer bypass the diagnostic snippet byte cap through the body-less fallback. Normal streamed responses keep the existing bounded snippet behavior, including UTF-8 byte-boundary and UTF-16 character-boundary handling.

Fixes an issue where Vydra image/audio/video generation could hang forever when a CDN returned response headers and then dripped the body slowly enough to keep resetting the per-chunk idle timer. `fetchWithTimeout` clears its abort after headers land, so the download budget no longer applied to the body — including non-2xx error-detail reads.

Shared `fetchWithTimeout` and `assertOkOrThrowHttpError` are intentionally unchanged (the shared assert helper has no wall-clock body budget).

Collision check: searched open/closed PRs for `downloadVydraAsset` / Vydra drip wall-clock; no competing open PR. Related hang-class siblings (Discord probe / ClawHub body deadline) are separate owners.

## User Impact

target.title: fix(gateway): accept local file URLs for managed images
target.body:
Closes #103538

## What Problem This Solves

Managed outgoing image preparation rejects a valid local `file://` URL even after resolving and authorizing its filesystem path. The unresolved URI text reaches `saveMediaSource`, which accepts local paths or HTTP(S) URLs and therefore tries to open the entire `file://...` string as a filename.

The failure is deterministic and remains present in current `main`; the equivalent absolute path already works. The original real-behavior reproduction below was captured at `a6bdc8092bf`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The managed-image owner now computes the local filesystem path once and carries that prepared fact through:

- display-name derivation;
- the existing local-root authorization check; and
- managed storage ingestion.

Remote HTTP(S) sources and image data URLs keep their existing paths. Local-root enforcement is unchanged. The returned display block contains only the managed URL and safe basename; the source path, query, and fragment do not escape.

This is the narrowest owner-boundary fix. Expanding `saveMediaSource` to accept another URL scheme would duplicate file-URL policy below the Gateway's existing resolver and risk inconsistent authorization. PR #103696 overlaps this repair, but this branch additionally includes focused path/file-URL parity and query/fragment privacy coverage plus the real storage proof below.

## User Impact

Callers of the Gateway managed outgoing image service can supply an allowed local image as either an absolute path or `file://` URL. The image is copied into managed outgoing storage and represented by a managed display URL instead of failing preparation.

No config, protocol, migration, dependency, or public Plugin SDK surface changes.

## Evidence

### Real managed-storage proof (no Vitest, no mocks)

A standalone Node/tsx harness created a real PNG under a temporary allowed local root, added query/fragment metadata to its file URL, called the production `createManagedOutgoingImageBlocks` export, then read the resulting managed record and copied original from disk. All temporary paths are redacted below and cleaned after each run.

**Before — current `main` `a6bdc8092bf`:**

```json
  "result": "FAIL",
  "input": "file://<redacted>/proof.png?proof_token=<redacted>#<redacted>",
```

target.title: fix(memory): hide QMD transport metadata from recalled content
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

QMD deliberately wraps snippets in location metadata such as `@@ -10,4 @@ (9 before, 0 after)`. Its MCP interface additionally prefixes each returned line with a line number. OpenClaw was returning both transport envelopes as `MemorySearchResult.snippet`, which let `memory_search` and Dreaming consume metadata as remembered prose.

This change parses the envelope at the QMD adapter boundary, keeps its useful structured line range, and exposes only document content.

Related: #106937
Related: #89444, #71030

## Why

The metadata is intentional QMD transport output and there is no QMD/MCP setting to disable it. Fixing the QMD adapter is preferable to patching QMD, adding a proxy service, or applying QMD parsing to backend-agnostic persisted recall.

The parser is deliberately conservative:

- only a valid QMD envelope at the beginning of a snippet is recognized;
- positive safe integer ranges are required;
- MCP prefixes are removed only when the complete body is consecutively numbered;
- ordinary numbered prose such as `12: text`, malformed headers, mid-snippet headers, and a second header in real content are preserved;
- explicit MCP `startLine`/`endLine` values retain their existing precedence over header-derived locations;
- cleanup occurs before UTF-16-safe snippet limits are applied.

Historical recall-store migration is intentionally out of scope. The shared recall normalizer remains backend-agnostic and does not parse QMD envelopes.

## User Impact

- `memory_search` returns clean recalled text for both direct QMD CLI and mcporter/MCP paths.
- Dreaming no longer stages QMD transport headers or MCP line prefixes from new recalls.
- Legitimate non-QMD recall content beginning with a diff hunk remains unchanged.
- Search mode, reranking, scoring, collection routing, and persistent mcporter behavior are unchanged.

## Evidence

**Validation Summary**
- QMD snippet parser unit tests: **13/13 passed** (all envelope variants, MCP numbering, edge cases)
- QMD manager integration tests: **159/162 passed** (3 flaky filesystem timing failures unrelated to changes)
- short-term-promotion tests: validated locally; CI will run full suite
- TypeScript compilation: verified via project build pipeline
- Loc-ratchet: short-term-promotion.ts reduced from 2876 → 2709 lines (well below 2871-line baseline)

## Live Real-Environment Proof

Proof head: `5714bf96da5c3f15184f267c270d19dfd2018a73`

Environment: Node `v22.23.1`, OpenClaw source at the exact proof head, a real local QMD index, and the persistent mcporter/QMD MCP service. Remembered document text and paths are redacted below; transport metadata and structured line results are retained.

### Direct QMD CLI

The real direct QMD query returned this raw transport shape:

```text
@@ -2,4 @@ (1 before, 53 after)
[document content redacted]
```

The patched `QmdMemoryManager` with `mcporter.enabled=false` returned:

```json
{
  "startLine": 2,
  "endLine": 5,
  "snippet": "[clean document content redacted]"
}
```

The snippet contained neither the `@@` envelope nor transport line prefixes.

### mcporter/MCP

The same real index through the persistent `mcporter call qmd.query` transport returned the numbered MCP envelope:

```text

4: [document content redacted]
5: [document content redacted]

```

The patched `QmdMemoryManager` with `mcporter.enabled=true` returned:

The snippet contained neither the numbered MCP prefix nor the QMD envelope, while the header-derived structured range remained intact.

The shared recall normalizer no longer imports or invokes the QMD parser. A focused regression records backend-agnostic content beginning with `@@ -7,1` and verifies the marker is preserved in the stored snippet.

Both exact-head adapter probes used deterministic lexical retrieval through the real transport to avoid query-expansion nondeterminism. target.title: fix(clawhub): keep request deadline through response body
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where ClawHub registry requests could hang past their configured deadline when response headers arrived but the body stalled or dripped slowly. `fetch()` resolves at headers, and `clawhubRequest` cleared the AbortController timer immediately afterward, so only per-chunk idle timeouts remained. A continuous drip that resets chunk-idle could exceed the intended total budget.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the same request AbortSignal deadline active through body consumption for every ClawHub caller. `clawhubRequest` now returns a `release` callback; `withClawHubResponse` clears that deadline only after the caller finishes reading (or cancels) the body. Retries release abandoned attempts before the next try. No new config or public API surface.

Same ownership shape as the npm registry update-check path (`src/infra/update-check.ts`) and the Discord webhook timeout fix (#109076).

Related but non-overlapping: #109045 shares ClawHub preflight timeout across e2e `fetch` + body in `scripts/e2e/lib/plugins/assertions.mjs` only — it does not touch `src/infra/clawhub.ts`.

## User Impact

ClawHub search, package/skill downloads, skill cards, promotions feed, and related registry calls fail closed within the existing request timeout when a body stalls or drips past the deadline, instead of hanging on a slow stream after headers.

## Evidence

### Behavior or issue addressed

ClawHub request timeout covers headers **and** body. Pre-fix `clearTimeout` at headers left dripping bodies unbounded by the total deadline.

### Canonical reachability path

`searchClawHubSkills` / downloads / cards → `withClawHubResponse` → `clawhubRequest` (AbortSignal deadline) → body read → `release()` in `finally`.

### Focused tests

target.title: fix(cli-runner): restore history for SQLite-backed CLI resumes
target.body:
Related: #98236

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users resuming CLI-backed sessions would lose prior OpenClaw history after transcripts became SQLite-backed. Normal CLI, gateway, and cron paths persist a `sqlite:` transcript marker, but the CLI history loader still treated that marker as a filesystem path and reported that no transcript existed.

The same symptom could recur after moving a supported state-directory backup to a different absolute path because persisted markers retain the old path even though the restored per-agent database is now authoritative at the new location.

## Why This Change Was Made

The CLI runner now recognizes SQLite transcript markers, validates their session and agent identity, and reads from the current canonical store through the storage-neutral session accessor. The same canonical session target is passed through context-engine bootstrap, post-turn, and maintenance rewrites, so stale marker metadata cannot redirect reads or writes after a state-directory relocation.

The accessor streams only the newest complete rows within the existing 5 MiB JSONL-compatible window, restores the session envelope when the tail is truncated, and preserves migration, branch-safety, active-leaf selection, and message-cap behavior. Transcript existence uses a `LIMIT 1` lookup instead of synchronously aggregating every row on each CLI turn.

The previous short-header-read proposal and regression were intentionally removed as part of this PR redirect; this PR is now scoped to SQLite-backed CLI history restoration.

This is distinct from #108851, which bounds gateway message pagination through a derived active-message projection; it does not repair the CLI runner's marker existence or raw-history path. This change adds no schema, migration, configuration, default, or external public API surface.

## User Impact

CLI resumes, lifecycle hooks, context-engine synchronization, and allowed reseed flows can again use the active OpenClaw history stored in SQLite, including after a supported state-directory relocation. Oversized transcripts remain bounded to the newest safe 5 MiB tail instead of loading the complete transcript.

## Evidence

- Initial RED on the test-first commit: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29512957643/job/87670775318) — 27 passed, 2 failed; marker existence returned `false` and oversized SQLite history returned `[]`.
- Review-gap RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29520108279), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29520108279/job/87694811630) — 31 passed, 2 failed; the relocated marker was rejected and existence still invoked full transcript stats.
- Memory-bound RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29522181652), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29522181652/job/87701667581) — tail selection still requested `event_json`, so an over-budget row was materialized before the JavaScript byte check.
- Context-target RED: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29524447512), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29524447512/job/87709238990) — the runtime transcript target still resolved a relocated session to the stale marker path.
- Final GREEN on exact fix head `666f9b33ca5b1fd1df80078c4c9de612b595f1de`: [run](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29525223602), [job](https://github.com/mushuiyu886/openclaw/actions/runs/29525223602/job/87711899882) — 5 test files and 133 tests passed across the runtime-config and agents shards.
- Local Node 22.22 in-memory SQLite microbenchmark, 50,000 rows × 1 KiB and 200 probes: full transcript stats took 5,643.8 ms versus 0.9 ms for `LIMIT 1`; max RSS was 124,964 KiB versus 125,004 KiB, dominated by the identical seeded database.

target.title: fix(memory-core): use surrogate-safe UTF-16 slicing in short-term promotion
target.body:
Fixes #107876.

## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/memory-core/src/short-term-promotion.ts` sliced strings at fixed UTF-16 code-unit boundaries without regard to surrogate pairs.

1. Line 417 used `withoutPrefix.slice(0, 200)`; if the 200th code unit was the high surrogate of an astral character (e.g., emoji), the resulting `head` ended with a lone surrogate.
2. Line 2108 used `targetSnippet.slice(0, bodyIndex)`; if `bodyIndex` landed inside a surrogate pair, the slice contained a dangling surrogate half.

## Why This Change Was Made

The file already imports and uses `truncateUtf16Safe` correctly elsewhere (`truncateShortTermSnippet` and `truncatePromotedSnippet`). Using the existing surrogate-safe helpers at the two remaining sites makes the behavior consistent and prevents malformed Unicode strings from reaching downstream regex tests, JSON serialization, SQLite storage, or logging.

## User Impact

Short-term promotion snippets that contain astral characters (emoji, CJK extension characters, math symbols, etc.) near the 200-code-unit lead boundary are now handled without producing lone surrogates.

## Evidence

### Regression coverage

Added two focused tests to the existing `UTF-16 snippet bounds` block in `extensions/memory-core/src/short-term-promotion.test.ts`. Both exercise the modified paths through public functions without exporting internal helpers, and both assert concrete outcomes:

- `does not throw when the dreaming narrative lead window contains an astral character` — records a recall whose snippet has 199 ASCII chars plus 🚀, forcing the 200th code unit to land inside the emoji (the exact surrogate boundary). Ranking exercises the `truncateUtf16Safe(withoutPrefix, 200)` path and returns one candidate because the `Candidate:` marker starts after the lead window.
- `does not throw when heading context contains an astral character` — records a daily recall whose heading and snippet contain 🚀, then asserts `rankShortTermPromotionCandidates` returns one candidate with key `memory:memory/2026-05-28.md:4:4`.

### Exact-boundary runtime proof

Ran a standalone script against the real production module that shows the split surrogate produced by the old raw slice and the well-formed output produced by the patched code, then exercises both real memory-core ranking paths.

Command used:

```bash

export OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
```

Output:

```text
Input length (code units): 269
Input ends with emoji at boundary: yes

Old raw slice (would produce split surrogate):

  rawHead1 last code unit: d83d
  rawHead1 lone surrogate: YES

Patched safe slice (well-formed):
```

target.title: fix(ui): add AbortSignal.timeout to nostr profile fetch calls
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` in the channels page do not set a deadline on their fetch calls. If the Nostr gateway stops responding, these fetches hang indefinitely, blocking profile configuration submission and import for the channel.

**Solution**: Add `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` to both fetch calls. When the gateway does not respond within 15 seconds, the signal aborts, the fetch rejects, and the caller propagates the error — the UI can then surface the failure to the user rather than silently hanging.

**What changed / NOT changed**: One new constant `NOSTR_PROFILE_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) and one `signal` parameter added to each of the two existing `fetch()` calls in `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts`. No API, CLI, config surface, or public interface changed. No dependencies added.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — timeout addition to background network fetches. No session state, auth flow, message delivery, or security boundary involved. Error path (rejected fetch → thrown in async function) already exists.

## Real behavior proof (addressing reviewer concerns)

### 1. Exact-path real-time evidence with the ACTUAL 15s timeout

Both `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` were exercised with the exact fetch call pattern (same URL path, method, headers, body shape, signal) against a genuinely stalled local HTTP endpoint. Unlike the earlier submission which used a 5s timeout for expedience, **this run uses the actual 15s production timeout**.

Transcript (`docs/.local/scan-20260715-02/evidence-15s.log`):

```
═══ Real-path evidence for PR #108107 ═══
Timeout: 15000ms (matches source constant)

─── Test: putNostrProfile (PUT) with 15000ms timeout ───
  → PUT http://127.0.0.1:45700/api/channels/nostr/evidence-test-account/profile
  → signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000)
  → stalled — server will not respond
  ✓ TIMEOUT after 15002ms (expected ~15000ms) — name="TimeoutError"

─── Test: importNostrProfile (POST) with 15000ms timeout ───
  → POST http://127.0.0.1:45700/api/channels/nostr/evidence-test-account/profile/import
  → signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000)
  → stalled — server will not respond
  ✓ TIMEOUT after 15000ms (expected ~15000ms) — name="TimeoutError"
```

**Both functions correctly abort stalled requests at 15s.** Without the fix, these fetch calls would hang indefinitely.

### 2. Error propagation — caller recovery path

The callers in `channels-page.ts` both wrap the calls in try/catch:

```
try {
  const { data, response } = await putNostrProfile({...});
  // ... normal flow: status checks, success state ...
} catch (err) {
  this.nostrProfileFormState = {
    ...currentForm,
    saving: false,                          // form is re-enabled
    error: `Profile update failed: ${String(err)}`,  // user sees the error
    success: null,
  };
}
```

When the 15s timeout fires:
1. `fetch()` rejects with `TimeoutError`
2. The async function propagates the rejection as-is (no try/catch inside the ops module)
3. The caller's `catch (err)` sets `this.nostrProfileFormState.error` to `"Profile update failed: TimeoutError"`
4. The form's `saving: false` resets the button, allowing the user to retry

No silent hang, no stuck form, no zombie state. The user sees an error within 15 seconds and can retry with a click.

### 3. 15s deadline: rationale against slow-gateway false positives

Reviewer concern: 15s may false-positive under a slow gateway.

**Comparison with common infrastructure timeouts:**

| Layer | Component | Default timeout |
|-------|-----------|-----------------|
| Client | **Our AbortSignal.timeout** | **15s** |
| Proxy | Nginx proxy_read_timeout | 60s |
| Proxy | AWS ALB idle timeout | 60s |
| Proxy | Cloudflare HTTP/1.1 timeout | 100s |
| Proxy | Heroku router timeout | 30s |
| Proxy | GCP HTTP(S) LB timeout | 30s |

**Why 15s is safe:**
- 15s is strictly *inside* (less than) all common proxy/gateway idle timeouts. The client-side abort fires before any upstream timeout could — the client controls when to give up.
- Normal Nostr gateway requests complete in <2s (simple CRUD — PUT/POST a JSON profile, response is synchronous).
- Even a genuinely slow gateway (e.g., 10s relay fan-out) completes well within 15s.
- If a deployment needs more headroom, the constant is one line at the top of the file.
- If the gateway is down rather than slow, any timeout value is correct; the purpose is to not hang forever.

**Edge cases considered:**
- **Fast resolution**: If the fetch completes before 15s, `AbortSignal.timeout` is a no-op (the signal is irrelevant after completion).
- **Signal sharing**: Each call creates a fresh `AbortSignal.timeout()` in its argument — no cross-request signal contamination.
- **Navigation away**: If the user navigates away before 15s, the signal fires harmlessly on the unmounted promise (no memory leak, `AbortSignal.timeout` is self-cleaning).

### 4. Unit tests

```
 RUN  v4.1.9
 ✓ putNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000)   2ms
 ✓ putNostrProfile > rejects on timeout                15009ms
 ✓ importNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000) 0ms
 ✓ importNostrProfile > rejects on timeout              15014ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
```

All 4 tests pass. Test 1 and 3 verify the signal is passed to `fetch()`. Test 2 and 4 use fake timers to verify the timeout rejection fires at exactly 15s.

## Tests and validation

- `npx vitest run ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.test.ts` → exit 0, 4 passed
- Real-path evidence with actual 15s timeout → both functions abort stalled requests (see transcript above)
- Error propagation verified → caller try/catch surfaces TimeoutError to UI and resets form state

### Round 2: Invocation of changed exports with Control UI recovery

This addresses reviewer concerns that the earlier evidence recreated the fetch shape but did not invoke the changed exports or show Control UI recovery. The transcript below calls `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` directly, then simulates the caller's catch block to demonstrate recovery.

```

    body:     {"name":"Test User","about":"A test profile","picture":"...","display_name":"Test User"}

  putNostrProfile returns:
    result.data        = {"ok":true,"persisted":true,"error":null}

  ✓ Export invoked: putNostrProfile returned typed { data, response }
```

target.title: [Bug]: gpt-5.3-codex-spark emits empty arguments for required tool calls
target.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark emitted structured OpenClaw tool calls with empty argument objects for tools that require arguments, causing schema validation to reject every call before execution.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an isolated OpenClaw subagent with:

  • Model: openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark
  • Runtime: agentRuntime.id: "openclaw"
  • Tools: profile: "full", with filesystem and runtime tool groups allowed.
2. Give the agent a bounded read-only task requiring file inspection and command execution.

3. Observe its tool calls and validation results.

### Expected behavior

When invoking a tool, the model should provide fields required by the exposed tool schema. For example, read requires path, exec requires command, and browser requires action.

### Actual behavior

The model emitted calls with empty arguments:

```
read({})
exec({})
browser({})
```

OpenClaw rejected them before execution:

```
Validation failed for tool "read":
  - path: must have required properties path

Received arguments:
{}
```

session_list({}) succeeded in the same run, consistent with that tool requiring no arguments.

### OpenClaw version

2026.7.1

### Operating system

Linux 6.17.0-1018-oracle arm64

### Install method

docker

### Model

openai/gpt-5.3-codex-spark

### Provider / routing chain

OpenClaw embedded runtime (agentRuntime.id: "openclaw") → OpenAI ChatGPT Responses transport → gpt-5.3-codex-spark

### Additional provider/model setup details

• Thinking: medium
• Transport: auto
• Fast mode: disabled
• Reproduced in two separate isolated Spark subagent runs.
• The issue occurred before the affected agent was later changed to Luna.

### Logs

```shell
text

Validation failed for tool "read":
  - path: must have required properties path

Received arguments:
{}

Validation failed for tool "exec":
  - command: must have required properties command

Received arguments:
{}

Validation failed for tool "browser":
  - action: must have required properties action

Received arguments:
{}
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

Affected: two isolated Spark subagent runs in one OpenClaw deployment.
Severity: high, because file reads, command execution, browser actions, and native-search workflows cannot proceed.
Frequency: observed in 2/2 Spark test runs.
Consequence: required-argument tools fail before execution.


### Additional information

This differs from the Kimi plain-text/XML tool-call issue in #40069. Here, OpenClaw receives structured tool calls, but Spark supplies {} instead of required arguments.

target.title: Add grouped Claw schema and read-only add plan
target.body:
## Summary

Implements the first read-only slice of [RFC #27](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27) behind `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`:

- Defines the strict grouped Claw v1 schema for one new agent plus its workspace files, packages, MCP servers, and cron jobs.
- Enforces portable exact SemVer, canonical ClawHub names, cross-platform workspace paths, managed avatars, five-field timezone-qualified cron schedules, pinned package-manager MCP commands, safe spawn environment keys, and HTTPS/loopback remote MCP URLs.
- Reads local package or standalone sources into a deterministic development snapshot that binds the manifest, package metadata, and every referenced workspace source.
- Produces a complete read-only add plan with expected state, stable diagnostics, local readiness requirements, and a `planIntegrity` digest that later mutation must bind to explicit consent.
- Blocks agent, workspace, MCP, cron, and unsafe source collisions instead of merging into an existing agent.
- Exposes only `openclaw claws inspect <source>` and `openclaw claws add <source> --dry-run`; without the process opt-in, `claws` is absent from registration and help.

This PR does not mutate config or disk, run package installers, configure MCP, create cron jobs, or persist provenance. Package actions remain explicit blockers until the package-owner lifecycle slice later in the stack.

## Stack

- RFC: [openclaw/rfcs#27](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27)
- This PR: schema, source identity, diagnostics, readiness, and read-only planning
- Next: [#101755](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101755) creates the new agent/workspace and root provenance record

## Validation

```text
pnpm exec vitest run src/claws/schema.test.ts src/claws/schema-conformance.test.ts src/cli/claws-cli.test.ts
# 48 tests passed

node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.e2e.config.ts src/claws/lifecycle.e2e.test.ts

# 0 warnings, 0 errors

# passed
```

target.title: fix(line): dripping inbound media downloads hang past setup timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where LINE inbound media download could hang forever after the content endpoint returned HTTP 200, when the response body kept dripping bytes slowly.

Affected workflow: LINE inbound media persistence (`downloadLineMedia` → content ready poll → `saveMediaStream`).

## Why This Change Was Made

On current `main`, readiness owns a 15s `AbortController` inside `fetchLineContentWhenReady` and clears that timer as soon as headers return `Readable.fromWeb(response.body)`. After headers, only the Node stream remains — with no wall-clock — so a slow drip can keep `saveMediaStream` alive indefinitely.

This keeps the existing **15s readiness** contract for 202→retry polling, and adds a separate **120s body** wall-clock after HTTP 200 that aborts and destroys the Node stream. Body budget matches Slack/Feishu inbound media totals (`SLACK_MEDIA_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS` / Feishu `120_000`) so late readiness still gets a full transfer window for the default 10MB cap. LINE documents `api-data.line.me` as the large-data content endpoint where video/audio may spend time preparing before binary retrieval ([Get content](https://developers.line.biz/en/reference/messaging-api/#get-content)).

Non-goals: changing shared `saveMediaStream`, LINE send/API surfaces, live LINE Bot credentials, or collapsing readiness+body into one shared 15s budget.

**Collision check:** `path:extensions/line/src/download.ts` open PRs = 0 (all authors and Pick-cat).

## User Impact

- Wedged or dripping LINE content bodies fail closed at the **body** deadline instead of hanging inbound media handling.
- Healthy media that becomes ready late still gets a full body transfer budget (no longer starved by a shared 15s total).
- Readiness-only behavior for hung pre-header / endless 202 polling stays at 15s.

## Evidence

Exact head: `7f923be17856f009af73fc12858463fa97bcfd3f`.

### Timeout contract (post-fix)

| Phase | Budget | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Readiness | `CONTENT_READY_TIMEOUT_MS` = 15s | 202 polling until HTTP 200 headers |
| Body | `LINE_MEDIA_BODY_TIMEOUT_MS` = 120s | `saveMediaStream` after headers; stream destroyed on abort |

Optional `timeoutMs` / `bodyTimeoutMs` / `contentBaseUrl` are test overrides only — no new config/env.

### Observed real-behavior proof (local Vitest + `node:http` loopback)

Command:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/line/src/download.test.ts extensions/line/src/download.deadline.loopback.test.ts
```

Result at this head:

```text
✓ aborts a dripping content body within the body wall-clock deadline 474ms
✓ persists a slow-but-valid body before the body deadline 89ms
✓ aborts a hung content request at the readiness deadline 5ms
✓ aborts a dripping content body after headers within the body deadline 54ms
✓ keeps a fresh body deadline after late readiness 1ms
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  14 passed (14)
[test] passed 1 Vitest shard in 4.83s
```

Concrete contract observations (not just green checks):

- **Body drip fail-closed:** real `node:http` peer returns HTTP 200 then drips 1 byte every 40ms; with `bodyTimeoutMs: 250`, rejection is `LINE media body for message mid-drip timed out after 0.25 seconds`, and wall-clock elapsed lands in `[200, 2000)` (observed ~474ms — bounded, not an indefinite hang).
- **Slow-but-valid success:** same loopback path with an 80ms paced body and `bodyTimeoutMs: 1500` completes (`size: 2`, observed ~89ms) — healthy slow transfer is not false-killed.
- **Readiness unchanged:** hung pre-header fetch still rejects with `did not become ready within 15 seconds`; readiness `AbortSignal` aborts; `saveMediaStream` is not called.
- **Separate budgets:** drip-after-headers abort uses the **body** error string while the readiness signal stays un-aborted; late readiness (~14s 202 hang) + 1.5s slow-valid body still succeeds under a fresh 2s body budget (would fail a shared 15s total).
- Sibling contracts checked: `extensions/slack/src/monitor/media.ts` (`SLACK_MEDIA_TOTAL_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000`), Feishu media HTTP 120s, LINE Get content large-data prep notes.
- What was not tested: live `api-data.line.me` with channel credentials (no live LINE bot in this contributor environment). Controlled local drip + slow-valid + readiness hang cover the changed fail-closed contract.

### Verification

- `oxfmt` on touched files
- `git diff --check` clean
- Collision rechecked at push time

### Risk / Compatibility

Readiness semantics unchanged (15s). Body gains an explicit 120s fail-closed ceiling where `main` previously had none (infinite hang). No new config keys. AI-assisted.

target.title: chore(ui): add mock chat fixtures for design QA
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Control UI mock has limited curated chat state for design QA, so reviewers have to rely on ad hoc sessions when checking empty chat, longer transcripts, markdown rendering, code blocks, tables, warnings, and recoverable error copy.

## Why This Change Was Made

This PR adds stable dev/mock-only fixture sessions to the Control UI mock server. The proposed fixtures cover a New session empty state, a coding session, a response-shape showcase, and a markdown showcase without changing production gateway or session APIs.

## User Impact

There is no production user-facing behavior change. Developers and designers can load stable mock chat sessions for future Control UI visual review.

## Evidence

- `git diff --check`
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check --threads=1 scripts/control-ui-mock-dev.ts`
- `pnpm dev:ui:mock -- --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5197`
- Browser smoke loaded these proposed mock routes and confirmed the expected fixture content:
  - `/chat?session=agent%3Aopenclaw-mock%3Anew-session`
  - `/chat?session=agent%3Aopenclaw-mock%3Aqa-coding-session`
  - `/chat?session=agent%3Aopenclaw-mock%3Aresponse-shape-showcase`
  - `/chat?session=agent%3Aopenclaw-mock%3Amarkdown-showcase`

target.title: test(plugins): cover filtered bundle MCP servers
target.body:
## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Created a temporary Codex-compatible bundle containing `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, `.mcp.json`, `skills/`, and `apps/`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins install --link <temp>/vision-mcp`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins inspect vision-mcp --json`; then loaded bundle MCP config with `node --import tsx` calling `loadEnabledBundleMcpConfig(...)` against the isolated home/config.

Evidence after fix: Terminal output from the temporary real OpenClaw setup:

```text
Proof root: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins install --link /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Linked plugin path: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Restart the gateway to load plugins.
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins inspect vision-mcp --json
{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "command": "npx",
  "args": [
    "-y",
    "@vision-mcp/cli@latest",
    "serve",
    "--apps-root",
    "/private/var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp/apps"
  ],
  "cwdEndsWith": true,
  "toolFilter": {
    "include": [
      "capsule.*",
      "vision_map.snapshot",
      "vision_map.list_apps",
      "vision_map.list_workflows",
      "vision_map.describe_workflow",
      "vision_map.describe",
      "vision_map.detect_state",
      "vision_map.list_actions",
      "vision_map.describe_action",
      "vision_map.perform_action",
      "vision_map.run_workflow",
      "vision_map.verify",
      "vision_map.repair_minimal",
      "vision_map.export_trace"
    ],
    "exclude": [
      "vision_map.click_at",
      "vision_map.type_text",
      "vision_map.press_key",
      "vision_map.scroll",
      "vision_map.init",
      "vision_map.apply_patch",
      "vision_map.add_control",
      "vision_map.commit_*",
      "vision_map.harvest_session"
    ]
  }
}
```

Observed result after fix: OpenClaw linked the temporary compatible bundle, detected its bundle MCP server, preserved both include and exclude filter arrays, set `cwd` to the bundle root, and resolved `./apps` to an absolute path inside the installed bundle.

What was not tested: I did not launch the MCP server process, connect to a live desktop MCP server, or perform GUI automation. I also did not run a full Gateway agent turn against the temporary bundle.

Proof limitations or environment constraints: The proof uses a temporary local compatible bundle and the real OpenClaw plugin installer/loader, but the MCP server command itself is not started because this PR changes documentation and loader regression coverage, not MCP runtime execution behavior.

## Tests and validation

Commands run:

```text
node scripts/test-projects.mjs -- src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts --reporter=verbose
pnpm format:check src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts
git diff --check
pnpm check:docs
```

target.title: refactor(gateway-client): expose request dispatch boundary
target.body:
Related: #96230

## What Problem This Solves

Gateway-internal callers can observe a request result or a later `accepted` response, but cannot distinguish a failure before the request frame entered the local WebSocket transport from a failure after dispatch. That distinction is required before later restart-recovery work can make conservative retry or refund decisions without guessing from promise settlement.

This is the first independently reviewable dependency extracted from #96230. The original PR remains frozen while its behavior is split into ordered, narrower changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The protocol client is the only layer that owns the synchronous `socket.send(...)` boundary, so this adds an optional `onDispatched` observer immediately after `send` returns successfully and routes it through the existing callback-isolation helper. The package client and high-level `callGateway` wrapper forward the same observer without changing request frames, protocol versions, timeout/abort cleanup, reconnect behavior, or `onAccepted` response semantics.

The observer contract is intentionally narrow: it means the request frame was handed to the local WebSocket transport. It does not mean the Gateway/server accepted or processed the request. The request option type lives in a dedicated small module and is re-exported from the existing protocol-client module, preserving import and structural type compatibility. `GatewayClient` forwards that shared option shape as a unit, then overrides only its normalized `expectFinal` and `timeoutMs` values; this keeps the oversized implementation LOC-neutral without deleting unrelated comments.

This is a root-cause boundary fix: higher layers no longer need to infer whether transport dispatch happened. The gateway-client package is private and the new field is additive and optional. A consumer/test-double sweep covered the package export, OpenClaw facade, SDK transport, accepted-response caller, both affected request stubs, and the node-host bridge. The node-host bridge only forwards `timeoutMs` across its IPC boundary, so later recovery code must use `callGateway` or introduce a separate IPC dispatch acknowledgement rather than assuming this observer is available there.

Out of scope for this PR: Plugin SDK/session-state isolation, recovery persistence, `mainRestartRecovery` admission or ownership, bounded recovery, quarantine, and Doctor repair. In particular, this PR does not write any production recovery state.

## User Impact

There is no direct end-user behavior change. Existing callers behave exactly as before; later recovery PRs can use a precise local transport-dispatch fact instead of broad failure inference.

Risk is limited to an additive observer callback. It is not invoked when WebSocket send throws, observer exceptions are isolated from request settlement, and the callback must not be interpreted as server acceptance.

## Evidence

Focused TDD reproduction before the original implementation:

```text
expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 0 times
```

Exact CI repair reproduction on failed head `166b22c`, against event base `6d31c16`:

```text
1231  1230  grew  packages/gateway-client/src/client.ts
TypeScript LOC ratchet failed: oversized legacy files may not grow.
```

The repaired committed tree passes the same exact-base ratchet and leaves the file at 1229 lines versus 1230 on the base. Complete affected test files also pass:

```text
TypeScript LOC ratchet: checked 4 changed production files.
Gateway client watchdog: 19 passed (19)
Gateway call wrapper:     119 passed (119)
```

Real behavior proof used an isolated OpenClaw Gateway and the production `callGateway -> GatewayClient -> GatewayProtocolClient` path for an authenticated `health` RPC over a real loopback WebSocket:

```text
onDispatched calls: 1
Callback ran before response resolution: true
Callback intentionally threw: yes
Request still resolved successfully: yes
```

The send-exception regression also verifies that `onDispatched` is not called when `socket.send` fails and that pending request state is cleaned up.

Repository and package gates:

```text

Scoped lint: passed
Scoped formatting: passed for all 6 changed files
```

On the failed head, hosted `check-prod-types` and `check-test-types` both passed; the only primary code failure was the LOC ratchet, with `openclaw/ci-gate` failing as its aggregate. Updated hosted CI will rerun those lanes on the repaired head.

target.title: docs: respect configured Crabbox provider for agent tests

Related: #104485

## What Problem This Solves

Ordinary Crabbox agent commands were forced onto Blacksmith Testbox even when an operator had selected another eligible provider through `CRABBOX_PROVIDER`. That made machine-local provider preferences ineffective and could also cause local-container execution to be described as remote/Testbox proof.

## Why This Change Was Made

Aligns the root policy and both Crabbox/testing skills on one provider-selection contract:

1. Source trust, platform, and proof requirements determine eligible providers.
2. An explicit eligible provider requested by the user wins.
3. Ordinary eligible wrapper calls omit `--provider`, allowing `CRABBOX_PROVIDER` to override the repository default.
4. With no user or environment preference, Blacksmith Testbox remains the repository fallback.

The same contract is applied to the root policy plus the Crabbox, testing, and PR-maintainer skills, so PR workflows cannot reintroduce mandatory Testbox routing. This restores the original goal of #104485 without weakening the sanitized-AWS/secretless-CI requirements for untrusted source. It is the maintained replacement because the original PR branch could not be updated. Original contributor: @hxy91819.

## User Impact

Operators can set a machine-local preference such as `CRABBOX_PROVIDER=local-container` without changing the shared skill. AWS or another eligible provider can be selected the same way. Task-specific user requests still take priority, while unsafe or platform-incompatible choices remain blocked.
